name: Aphids
description: Soft-bodied sap-suckers a millimetre or two long, in colonies on the newest growth and the undersides of leaves. They reproduce without mating and give birth to live young, so a handful in April is hundreds by the end of the month.
signs: Curled, puckered or cupped new leaves. Sticky honeydew on the leaves below, and black sooty mould growing on it. Ants running up and down the stem. White cast skins that look like the aphids themselves.
consequence: Rarely kills an established plant, but it stunts seedlings, deforms new growth and makes a leafy crop unsaleable and unpleasant. The real cost is virus: aphids move mosaic and leaf-curl viruses between plants in seconds of probing, and a virus cannot be treated once it is in.
look_alikes: Whiteflies fly up in a cloud when the plant is shaken; aphids do not. Leafhoppers scuttle sideways. Curling from herbicide drift affects the whole plant at once and has no insects on it.
monitoring: Turn over the top three leaves of a few plants twice a week from the first warm spell, and again in autumn. Ants climbing a stem are the cheapest sign there is, and they are usually there before you can see an aphid.
prevention: Do not overfeed with nitrogen: soft fast growth is exactly what they breed on. Leave a flowering strip or let some coriander and dill bolt, which is what feeds the predators. Reflective mulch keeps them off young plants.
organic_controls: A hard jet of water knocks a colony off and most never climb back; repeat every few days. Insecticidal soap or horticultural oil sprayed on the undersides where they actually are, repeated after a week. Pinch out and bin the worst shoot tips. Deal with the ants, which farm aphids and drive the predators off.
chemical_controls: Active ingredients registered for garden use include pyrethrins, azadirachtin from neem, and malathion. Avoid systemic neonicotinoids such as imidacloprid on anything that flowers or that bees visit; the residue is in the pollen for weeks.
beneficials: Ladybird adults and larvae, lacewing larvae, hoverfly larvae, and parasitic wasps. A papery bronze aphid stuck to a leaf is a parasitised one -- leave it, it is a wasp nursery.
treatments: Water jet, insecticidal soap or horticultural oil on the leaf undersides; deal with the ants; leave the ladybirds and the mummies alone.

name: Spider mites
description: Not insects but mites, less than half a millimetre across. They thrive in hot, dry, dusty weather and a generation takes about a week at 30C, which is why an outbreak seems to arrive overnight in July.
signs: Fine pale stippling on the upper leaf surface that goes bronze or grey. Fine webbing across leaf undersides and shoot tips. Leaves dropping from the bottom of the plant upward. Tap a leaf over white paper: the specks that walk are mites.
consequence: Heavy feeding takes away the plant's photosynthesis in exactly the weeks it should be filling fruit. Beans and melons can be killed outright; a tomato usually survives with a much smaller crop and sunscalded fruit where the canopy went.
look_alikes: Thrips and lace bugs also stipple, but leave no webbing. Ozone injury and magnesium deficiency stipple or bronze without any mites under a hand lens -- always look before spraying.
monitoring: From the first hot dry spell, check the undersides of lower leaves weekly with a hand lens. Dusty plants at the end of a row or beside a path are where it starts, every time.
prevention: Keep plants watered: drought-stressed plants are the ones that get hit. Hose dust off foliage in a dry spell. Avoid broad-spectrum insecticides, which kill the predatory mites and reliably cause the outbreak they were meant to prevent.
organic_controls: Spray water forcefully on the leaf undersides every few days. Horticultural oil or insecticidal soap, thoroughly, twice a week apart, because neither touches the eggs. Release predatory mites under cover. Remove and bag the worst leaves rather than shaking them over the row.
chemical_controls: Garden miticides carry active ingredients such as sulfur, or bifenthrin among the synthetics. Pyrethroids are known to flare mite populations by killing their predators, so they are the wrong reach here. Never apply sulfur or oil in heat, and never within two weeks of each other: the combination burns leaves.
beneficials: Predatory mites (Phytoseiulus, Neoseiulus), minute pirate bugs, sixspotted thrips, and the spider mite destroyer lady beetle.
treatments: Water on the undersides; oil or soap twice, a week apart; keep the plants watered; do not reach for a pyrethroid.

name: Whiteflies
description: Tiny white moth-like sap-suckers that rise in a cloud when a plant is disturbed and settle straight back. The scale-like nymphs on the leaf undersides do most of the feeding and do not move at all.
signs: A cloud of white specks off the foliage when you brush past. Sticky honeydew and sooty mould. Yellowing and silvering of leaves. On tomato, irregular ripening -- the fruit stays hard and white inside.
consequence: A heavy population weakens the plant and coats the crop in mould, but the reason to take it seriously is virus: whiteflies transmit tomato yellow leaf curl and the cucurbit yellowing viruses, and those end the planting.
look_alikes: Whitefly adults look like tiny white moths; a true moth is bigger and does not settle in seconds. The nymphs are easily mistaken for scale insects or for leaf spots until you look under a lens.
monitoring: Yellow sticky cards at canopy height catch them before the cloud is obvious. Check leaf undersides on transplants BEFORE you plant them: bought-in plants are how most gardens get them.
prevention: Inspect nursery plants and reject any with white specks underneath. Row cover on young plants. Remove and bag old infested crops rather than leaving them as a bridge to the next planting. Reflective mulch confuses the incoming adults.
organic_controls: Vacuum the adults in the cool of the morning when they are sluggish. Insecticidal soap or horticultural oil on the undersides, repeated, since neither reaches the eggs. Yellow sticky traps for the adults. Pull and bag the worst plants -- one heavily infested plant reinfests a whole bed.
chemical_controls: Insecticidal soap and horticultural oil are the mainstays; azadirachtin and pyrethrins are also registered. Whiteflies develop resistance quickly, so alternating chemistries matters more here than almost anywhere else. Avoid systemic neonicotinoids on flowering crops.
beneficials: Encarsia and Eretmocerus parasitic wasps, lacewing larvae, minute pirate bugs, and big-eyed bugs.
treatments: Soap or oil on leaf undersides, repeated; sticky traps; bag heavily infested plants; check every transplant before it goes in.

name: Thrips
description: Slender insects barely a millimetre long that rasp at leaf and petal tissue and drink what runs out. They shelter deep in buds and flowers, which is why a spray so often seems not to have worked.
signs: Silvery streaks and flecks on leaves with tiny black varnish-like specks of frass in them. Deformed, scarred fruit. Onion leaves silvered from the base up. Shake a flower over white paper and watch for slivers that run.
consequence: Direct feeding scars fruit and checks onions badly in a dry year. The larger risk is tomato spotted wilt virus, which thrips carry and which has no cure: an infected plant is pulled, not treated.
look_alikes: The silvering resembles spider mite stippling, but there is no webbing and the frass specks are diagnostic. Wind scarring on young fruit looks similar and has no insects behind it.
monitoring: Blue or yellow sticky cards, plus tapping flowers and onion leaf sheaths over white paper weekly from the first flowers. Populations spike when nearby weeds or grass are cut and the thrips move in.
prevention: Control weeds around the bed, but do not mow them off all at once in mid-season. Keep onions well watered. Use spotted-wilt-resistant tomato varieties where the virus is known. Reflective mulch delays arrival on young plants.
organic_controls: Insecticidal soap and spinosad both work but only reach the ones out in the open, so repeat treatments are the rule. Remove and bag spotted-wilt plants the day you find them. Sticky cards reduce a light population and tell you when to act on a heavy one.
chemical_controls: Spinosad is the most effective active ingredient available to a garden. It is highly toxic to bees while wet and effectively harmless once dry, so it is applied at dusk and never on open flowers. Pyrethrins are registered; thrips resistance is widespread.
beneficials: Minute pirate bugs, predatory mites (Amblyseius), lacewing larvae.
treatments: Spinosad or insecticidal soap, at dusk and repeated; sticky cards; pull and bag any plant showing spotted wilt.

name: Flea beetles
description: Small dark beetles, two or three millimetres, that jump like fleas when disturbed. They overwinter as adults in leaf litter and hedge bottoms and arrive on the first warm days, which is exactly when seedlings are smallest.
signs: Leaves shot through with round pinholes, heaviest at the edges of a bed and on the youngest leaves. In a bad year a seedling looks like lace.
consequence: A mature plant shrugs it off. A seedling does not: flea beetles are one of the few pests that reliably kill a stand of brassicas or eggplant outright in the first fortnight after emergence.
look_alikes: Slug damage is ragged-edged, not round, and comes with slime. Hail makes bigger, more irregular holes and tears leaf edges.
monitoring: Look at direct-sown brassicas and eggplant transplants every day for the first two weeks. Yellow sticky cards at soil level catch the first arrivals before the holes appear.
prevention: Floating row cover from the day of sowing, sealed at the edges, is close to complete control and is the answer for direct-sown brassicas. Transplant larger, hardened plants rather than sowing in place where the pressure is known. Delay planting past the first spring flush. Clear leaf litter and weedy edges over winter.
organic_controls: Row cover, and it can stay on brassicas all season because they need no pollinator. Trap crops of a preferred host at the end of the bed. Kaolin clay makes leaves unpalatable. Spinosad and pyrethrins are both registered and both work on a heavy attack.
chemical_controls: Spinosad, pyrethrins and carbaryl are registered for garden use against flea beetles. Spinosad is toxic to bees while wet, so it goes on at dusk; carbaryl is highly toxic to bees and should not be used on anything in flower.
beneficials: Ground beetles, big-eyed bugs, and braconid wasps that parasitise the adults.
treatments: Row cover from day one is the whole answer for seedlings; kaolin clay or spinosad at dusk when they are already in.

name: Cucumber beetles
also_called: Striped cucumber beetle; spotted cucumber beetle
description: Yellow beetles about six millimetres long, either with three black stripes or with twelve spots. They feed on leaves, flowers and rinds, and the striped species carries the bacterium that causes bacterial wilt in its gut over winter.
signs: Chewed leaves and ragged flowers on young cucurbits. Beetles inside the flowers in the morning. Scarring on melon and squash rinds. Later, a vine that wilts in the heat and does not recover overnight.
consequence: The chewing is survivable. Bacterial wilt is not: an infected cucumber or muskmelon vine dies, there is no treatment, and a handful of beetles feeding on a seedling is enough to do it. This is the pest that ends cucumber crops.
look_alikes: The spotted species is easily mistaken for a ladybird -- count the spots and look at the colour: a ladybird is domed and orange-red, this is flatter and yellow-green.
monitoring: Check every cucurbit seedling daily from emergence until it is running. Look inside the flowers at first light, which is where they shelter. Any beetle at all on a seedling is worth acting on.
prevention: Row cover from sowing until the first female flowers, then off for pollination -- this is the single most effective thing available. Delay planting past the first emergence. Grow butternut and other Cucurbita moschata types, which are far less susceptible to wilt. Yellow sticky traps at the bed edge.
organic_controls: Row cover until flowering. Hand-picking morning and evening while numbers are low. Kaolin clay on the seedlings. Perimeter trap cropping with a preferred squash around the main planting. Pull and bag a wilting vine at once so it is not a reservoir.
chemical_controls: Pyrethrins, spinosad and carbaryl are registered for garden use. All three are hazardous to bees, and cucurbits depend entirely on bees, so any application goes on at dusk when the flowers have closed and never in the morning when they are open and being worked.
beneficials: Tachinid flies parasitise the adults; soldier beetles, ground beetles and braconid wasps take eggs and larvae.
treatments: Row cover to first flower, then hand-pick and use kaolin clay; spray only at dusk, and pull wilting vines the day you see them.

name: Squash bugs
description: Flat grey-brown true bugs about 15 mm long that suck sap from stems and leaves and inject a toxin as they do it. The nymphs are grey with black legs and cluster in groups; the bronze, football-shaped eggs are laid in neat rows in the V of leaf veins.
signs: Bronze egg clusters on leaf undersides in the angle of the veins. Yellow speckling on leaves that goes brown and crisp. Wilting that starts at one runner. A sharp smell when a bug is crushed.
consequence: A young plant can be killed. An established one loses runners one at a time until the crop stops. They are also the vector of cucurbit yellow vine decline, which kills outright.
look_alikes: Very easily confused with the brown marmorated stink bug -- squash bugs are narrower with a more rectangular body, and they are on cucurbits and almost nothing else.
monitoring: Check leaf undersides twice a week from the moment the plants run, looking for the egg rows rather than the adults. Lay a board or a shingle flat on the soil beside the plant: the adults gather under it overnight and can be collected at dawn.
prevention: Row cover until flowering. Clear and compost old vines promptly -- the adults overwinter in crop debris. Avoid heavy loose mulch right at the crown, which is where they hide. Rotate cucurbits away from last year's ground.
organic_controls: Scrape the egg masses off with a fingernail or lift them with tape; this is genuinely the most effective control and it takes minutes a week. Board traps at dawn. Insecticidal soap on the small grey nymphs, which is the only stage it works on -- an adult's back sheds it.
chemical_controls: Pyrethrins, permethrin and carbaryl are registered. All are most effective against nymphs and largely wasted on adults, and all are hazardous to bees on a crop that cannot set fruit without them, so evening applications only.
beneficials: The tachinid fly Trichopoda pennipes -- a white egg glued to a squash bug's back is that fly, so leave those bugs where they are. Ground beetles take the eggs.
treatments: Scrape off the egg rows weekly; board traps at dawn; soap on the nymphs only; clear old vines in autumn.

name: Squash vine borer
description: A day-flying clearwing moth that looks like a wasp lays single eggs at the base of squash stems; the larva bores in and eats the stem out from the inside. There is one main generation in the north and often two further south.
signs: A vine that wilts in the afternoon and recovers, then wilts and does not. Sawdust-like frass, wet and orange, at the stem base or a leaf joint. A ragged hole in the stem. Cut the stem open lengthways and the fat white grub is inside.
consequence: The plant dies, usually just as it starts to crop, and no treatment reaches a larva already inside. This is the single most reliable way to lose summer squash and pumpkins east of the Rockies.
look_alikes: Bacterial wilt from cucumber beetles wilts a vine with no frass and no hole. Squash bug damage wilts one runner at a time from the leaf end, not the base.
monitoring: Timing is the whole game. Adults emerge at roughly 1000 growing degree days on a 50F base accumulated from 1 January, which is late April to early May in central Texas and June further north. Yellow bowls of water catch the adults and tell you the flight has begun.
prevention: Row cover from planting until the first female flowers, removed for pollination -- if the flight is over by then, the crop is safe. Sow a second, later planting to grow through the flight. Grow Cucurbita moschata types such as butternut and tromboncino, whose dense solid stems the larvae usually cannot complete development in. Mound soil over leaf joints so the vine roots along its length and survives one severed stem.
organic_controls: Wrap the lower 30 cm of stem in foil or old stocking so the female cannot lay on it. Inject Bacillus thuringiensis kurstaki into the stem base weekly during the flight, before the larva is deep. Surgery works: slit the stem lengthways with a razor, remove the grub, and bury the wounded section so it roots.
chemical_controls: Nothing reaches a larva inside a stem, so any spray is aimed at the adult during the flight and at the base of the plant. Registered garden actives include permethrin and carbaryl; both are hazardous to bees, and squash needs bees, so evenings only.
beneficials: Few. Parasitoids exist but do not hold it below damaging levels in a garden.
treatments: Row cover through the flight, moschata varieties, foil at the stem base, Bt injected weekly, and surgery when it is already in.

name: Pickleworm
description: A moth caterpillar of the warm south-east that bores into cucurbit flowers and then into the fruit. It does not overwinter far north and arrives later each season the further north you are, which is why an early crop escapes it.
signs: A small hole in the fruit with wet green-brown frass pushed out of it. Buds and flowers chewed out. Cut the fruit open and the caterpillar, pale green with dark spots when young, is in the flesh.
consequence: The fruit is ruined and the damage is invisible until you pick it. In a bad year on a late planting almost nothing is fit to eat.
look_alikes: The entry hole is easily mistaken for stink bug feeding, which leaves a pinprick and no frass.
monitoring: Check flowers and small fruit twice a week from midsummer. The first sign is chewed blossoms, before any fruit is holed.
prevention: Plant early and harvest before the population builds -- this is the main control and it is free. Row cover over an autumn planting until flowering. Remove and bin infested fruit rather than composting it. Butternut and other C. moschata types are less preferred.
organic_controls: Bacillus thuringiensis kurstaki applied to blossoms and small fruit in the evening, repeated weekly through the flight, catches the larvae before they bore in. Pick and destroy holed fruit.
chemical_controls: Spinosad and pyrethrins are registered for garden use. Both must reach the larva before it enters the fruit, so timing to the blossom stage matters more than the choice. Both are hazardous to bees while wet -- apply at dusk.
beneficials: Generalist predators only; nothing reliable once the larva is inside.
treatments: Plant early; Bt or spinosad on blossoms in the evening through the flight; bin holed fruit.

name: Tomato and tobacco hornworm
description: Very large green caterpillars, up to 10 cm, with diagonal stripes and a curved horn at the tail. Two or three eat more foliage in a night than everything else in the bed put together, and they are extraordinarily hard to see.
signs: Whole leaves and even stems stripped, from the top of the plant down. Dark green-black droppings the size of a peppercorn on leaves and soil below -- look for the frass first, then look straight up.
consequence: Defoliation of a plant or two, which a healthy tomato recovers from but which exposes the fruit to sunscald. Rarely fatal, always dramatic.
look_alikes: Nothing else is this size. The two species differ in the colour of the horn and the shape of the stripes, and it makes no practical difference.
monitoring: Walk the tomatoes twice a week looking for frass and stripped stems rather than for the caterpillar. A UV torch after dark makes them glow, and is by far the fastest way to find them.
prevention: Rotate away from last year's tomato ground -- they pupate in the soil beneath. Light cultivation after the crop destroys the pupae.
organic_controls: Hand-picking is the whole answer in a garden: drop them in soapy water, or move them to a wild host if you would rather. Bacillus thuringiensis kurstaki works well on small larvae and not at all on a fully grown one.
chemical_controls: Bt is the right tool and is the least disruptive thing on the shelf. Spinosad also works. Broad-spectrum insecticides are a poor trade here: they take the wasps that parasitise the hornworms with them.
beneficials: Braconid wasps. A hornworm covered in white rice-like cocoons has been parasitised -- leave it exactly where it is; those wasps are the next generation of control.
treatments: Hand-pick, using a UV torch after dark; Bt on small larvae; leave any hornworm carrying white cocoons.

name: Imported cabbageworm
description: The velvety green caterpillar of the small white butterfly you see flitting over the brassica bed all summer. It feeds slowly and constantly and hides along the midrib, where it is exactly the colour of the leaf.
signs: Irregular holes chewed in leaves, then into the head. Dark green pellets of frass caught in the leaf axils and in the broccoli head. White butterflies over the bed at midday.
consequence: Cosmetic on a big cabbage, ruinous on broccoli and cauliflower where the frass and the caterpillars end up inside the head and cannot be washed out.
look_alikes: Cabbage loopers arch their backs as they walk; these do not. Diamondback moth larvae are much smaller and wriggle violently and drop on a thread when touched.
monitoring: Check the growing point and the undersides of the top leaves twice a week from the first white butterfly. Bright yellow eggs, laid singly and standing on end, are the earliest sign.
prevention: Insect netting or floating row cover from planting: brassicas need no pollinator, so it can stay on all season and this is close to complete control. Do not plant new brassicas immediately beside a finishing crop.
organic_controls: Row cover. Hand-picking, which is easy once you learn to look along the midrib. Bacillus thuringiensis kurstaki sprayed on the growing point every week or so while butterflies are flying; it is specific to caterpillars and harms nothing else.
chemical_controls: Bt kurstaki is the right answer and is what extension programmes recommend first. Spinosad also works and goes on at dusk. Pyrethrins and permethrin are registered but take the parasitic wasps with them.
beneficials: Cotesia parasitic wasps, paper wasps -- which hunt caterpillars all day and are worth tolerating near a brassica bed -- and ground beetles.
treatments: Netting from planting; hand-pick along the midrib; Bt kurstaki weekly while the whites are flying.

name: Cabbage looper
description: A pale green caterpillar with a thin white stripe down each side that arches its back into a loop as it walks, having no legs in the middle. It has a much wider host range than the cabbageworm and turns up on lettuce and tomato as well.
signs: Large ragged holes between the veins, often leaving the leaf skeletal. Loose green frass. Caterpillars that loop when they move.
consequence: Defoliation and contaminated heads. A late-season problem more often than an early one, and rarely fatal to the plant.
look_alikes: Imported cabbageworm is velvety and does not loop. Beet armyworm is greyer and has a dark spot behind the head.
monitoring: Same walk as for cabbageworm: growing point and top leaf undersides twice a week. Pale green dome-shaped eggs laid singly.
prevention: Row cover on brassicas. Clear crop residue after harvest. Do not overlap successive brassica plantings in adjacent beds.
organic_controls: Row cover and hand-picking. Bacillus thuringiensis kurstaki while the larvae are small; loopers become notably harder to kill once large.
chemical_controls: Bt kurstaki first, spinosad second. Loopers have developed resistance to several older synthetics, which is another reason to start with Bt and rotate.
beneficials: Trichogramma egg wasps, Copidosoma parasitoids, paper wasps, and a naturally occurring nuclear polyhedrosis virus that collapses heavy populations on its own.
treatments: Netting; hand-pick; Bt kurstaki while the caterpillars are small.

name: Diamondback moth
description: The smallest of the three brassica caterpillars, under a centimetre, pale green and tapering at both ends. Disturb one and it thrashes wildly and drops on a silk thread, which is the surest way to identify it.
signs: Small windowpane patches where the larva has eaten one leaf surface and left the other, later becoming shot holes. Fine webbing on the growing point.
consequence: Minor on a mature plant, serious on transplants and on the growing point of broccoli. It matters mostly because it is the brassica pest most prone to insecticide resistance.
look_alikes: The windowpane feeding is distinctive; both other brassica caterpillars chew right through.
monitoring: Look at the growing point of young brassicas weekly. The dropping-on-a-thread behaviour identifies it instantly.
prevention: Row cover. Rotate brassica beds. Avoid repeated sprays of the same chemistry, which is precisely how resistant populations arise in this species.
organic_controls: Row cover and Bacillus thuringiensis. Where Bt resistance is suspected locally, spinosad is the alternative -- and alternating between the two is the point, not choosing one.
chemical_controls: Bt kurstaki or aizawai, and spinosad. This species has developed resistance to nearly every insecticide class used against it somewhere in the world; rotate actives and never spray on a schedule instead of on a count.
beneficials: Diadegma and Microplitis parasitic wasps, which do a great deal of unnoticed work and are the first thing a broad-spectrum spray removes.
treatments: Row cover; Bt and spinosad, alternated rather than repeated.

name: Cutworms
description: Fat, greasy-looking grey or brown caterpillars that curl into a C when touched. They live in the top few centimetres of soil, feed at night, and chew through the stems of young plants at ground level.
signs: A transplant lying cut clean off at soil level, still green. Gaps in a newly emerged row. Dig a few centimetres down within a hand's width of the stump and the caterpillar is usually there.
consequence: Whole transplants lost, one a night, until the caterpillar is found. In a bad spring on ground that was in grass last year, a third of a bed.
look_alikes: A rabbit clips a stem at an angle and leaves the top; a cutworm severs it flat and leaves the top lying. Damping-off collapses a seedling without cutting it.
monitoring: Walk newly transplanted beds every morning for the first fortnight and count the losses. Search the soil beside any cut stem before nightfall.
prevention: A collar around each transplant stem -- a toilet roll tube, a tin can with the ends out, or a strip of card pushed 3 cm into the soil -- is the single most reliable control and Carl records it on the planting. Cultivate a new bed two weeks before planting, especially ground that was in grass or weeds. Keep a clean, weed-free border.
organic_controls: Collars. Hand-searching at dusk with a torch. Bacillus thuringiensis kurstaki drenched on the soil surface at dusk. Diatomaceous earth as a barrier ring, renewed after rain.
chemical_controls: Baits containing spinosad or carbaryl are the usual garden option and are applied to the soil surface at dusk, when the larvae come up. Foliar sprays are largely wasted on a pest that is underground by dawn.
beneficials: Ground beetles, birds, parasitic wasps and tachinid flies.
treatments: A collar on every transplant; search at dusk; Bt or a spinosad bait on the soil surface in the evening.

name: Armyworms
description: Caterpillars that arrive in numbers rather than singly, marching through a planting and stripping it. Fall armyworm has a pale inverted Y on the head and four dots in a square on the second-to-last segment; beet armyworm has a dark spot above the second true leg.
signs: Ragged skeletonised leaves and a great deal of frass, appearing across a whole bed within a few days. On sweet corn, chewed whorls and damaged ear tips.
consequence: A planting can be stripped in under a week. Sweet corn ears are directly damaged and unmarketable.
look_alikes: Corn earworm is usually alone in the ear tip; armyworms are many and are in the whorl and the foliage.
monitoring: Check the corn whorl and the youngest leaves of everything else twice a week from midsummer. Egg masses come in furry grey clusters on leaf undersides -- crush those and the outbreak does not happen.
prevention: Plant early where the species is a late-season migrant. Keep the bed weed-free, since grassy weeds host the early generations. Destroy egg masses on sight.
organic_controls: Bacillus thuringiensis while larvae are small and still on the leaf surface, which is a narrow window. Hand-pick egg masses and young clusters. Spinosad on a heavier attack, at dusk.
chemical_controls: Spinosad and Bt aizawai are the effective garden actives; older synthetics are widely resisted by fall armyworm. Nothing reaches a larva already inside a corn ear, so timing to the whorl stage decides the outcome.
beneficials: Trichogramma egg wasps, tachinid flies, ground beetles, birds.
treatments: Crush egg masses; Bt or spinosad while the larvae are small and in the whorl; nothing works once they are in the ear.

name: Corn earworm
description: One species with three names, because it eats the ear of corn, the fruit of a tomato and the pod of a bean. Eggs are laid on fresh corn silk; the larva follows the silk down and feeds in the ear tip, and by then it is beyond reach.
signs: Chewed, frass-packed corn ear tips. Round holes in green tomatoes with frass at the entry. Larvae varying from pale green to brown with fine stripes.
consequence: Almost every unprotected sweet corn ear carries one in the south. In the ear tip it is a nuisance you cut off; in a tomato or a pepper it ruins the fruit and the rot follows it in.
look_alikes: In tomatoes the entry hole resembles stink bug feeding, which leaves no frass and no tunnel.
monitoring: Watch for fresh silk: that is the moment eggs are laid and the only moment anything can be done. On tomatoes, check green fruit weekly from first set.
prevention: Plant early so silking is over before the peak flight. Choose sweet corn varieties with tight husk tips. Cultivate after harvest to break up the pupae in the soil.
organic_controls: A few drops of vegetable oil, sometimes with Bacillus thuringiensis in it, applied to the silk channel a few days after silking, smothers the larva before it enters. A clothes peg or elastic band on the husk tip is a cruder version of the same idea. Bt or spinosad on tomatoes catches the larvae before they bore in.
chemical_controls: Spinosad and Bt are the garden actives, and both are applied to fresh silk or to green fruit -- nothing reaches a larva that is already inside. Bt is harmless to bees; spinosad is acutely toxic to them while it is wet and harmless once dry, so it goes on at dusk and never on open tomato or bean flowers. Repeated applications during silking are what commercial growers do and what a garden usually will not.
beneficials: Trichogramma egg wasps, minute pirate bugs on the silk, lacewings.
treatments: Oil or Bt on fresh corn silk; Bt or spinosad on green tomatoes; accept the ear tip and cut it off.

name: Colorado potato beetle
description: A round yellow beetle with ten black stripes and a brick-red humpbacked larva with two rows of black spots. Both stages eat foliage, and the larvae do most of the damage. It is famously quick to develop insecticide resistance.
signs: Yellow-orange egg clusters standing on end under the leaves. Foliage eaten to the stems from the top down. Both beetles and larvae plainly visible.
consequence: Complete defoliation of potatoes and eggplant, and on eggplant it will kill a young plant. Potatoes defoliated before tubers bulk yield almost nothing.
look_alikes: The false potato beetle has one white stripe among the black; the striping pattern is the tell. The larvae are unmistakable.
monitoring: Check the undersides of potato and eggplant leaves weekly from emergence for the orange egg clusters, which is the stage worth acting on.
prevention: Rotate potatoes and eggplant as far from last year's bed as the garden allows -- the adults walk out of the soil and a long walk stops many. Deep straw mulch makes that walk much harder. Plant early varieties and get them out.
organic_controls: Hand-picking adults and crushing egg clusters, which in a garden is genuinely sufficient. Straw mulch. Bacillus thuringiensis tenebrionis, which is the strain specific to beetles and not the kurstaki one sold for caterpillars. Spinosad on young larvae.
chemical_controls: Bt tenebrionis and spinosad are the effective garden actives. This species has developed resistance to more than fifty insecticides; never spray the same active twice in a season.
beneficials: Stink bugs of the genus Podisus, ground beetles, ladybirds eating the eggs.
treatments: Crush the orange egg clusters and hand-pick; straw mulch; Bt tenebrionis or spinosad on small larvae.

name: Mexican bean beetle
description: A ladybird that eats plants rather than aphids: coppery-orange with sixteen black spots, with spiny yellow larvae. Both stages feed on the undersides of bean leaves.
signs: Leaves skeletonised from below into a fine lace while the upper surface stays intact. Yellow egg clusters and spiny yellow grubs underneath.
consequence: Severe defoliation just as pods fill, which cuts the crop sharply. Successive generations get worse through the season.
look_alikes: Looks like a large ladybird, which is exactly the problem: check the colour, which is coppery rather than red, and check what it is doing.
monitoring: Look under bean leaves weekly from first true leaves. The yellow egg clusters are the stage to act on.
prevention: Plant early and harvest an early crop before numbers build. Pull and destroy the vines as soon as picking is over rather than leaving them standing. Row cover until flowering.
organic_controls: Hand-picking adults, larvae and egg clusters. Insecticidal soap or neem on the young larvae, on the undersides. Pediobius foveolatus, a parasitic wasp, is sold for this pest and works well where it is available.
chemical_controls: Pyrethrins and neem are the usual garden options and both are far more effective on larvae than on adults. Beans are visited by bees, so evening applications only.
beneficials: Pediobius foveolatus, spined soldier bugs, lady beetles taking the eggs.
treatments: Hand-pick adults, larvae and egg clusters; soap or neem on the undersides; pull the vines as soon as picking ends.

name: Bean leaf beetle
description: A small beetle, red to yellow-tan, usually with four dark spots and always with a small black triangle just behind the head -- the triangle is the reliable mark, since the spots are often absent.
signs: Round holes chewed between the veins of bean leaves. Later in the season, scarring and pitting on the pods themselves.
consequence: Leaf feeding is cosmetic on an established plant but can kill seedlings. Pod scarring lets in the fungi that cause pod rot, which is the real cost.
look_alikes: Cucumber beetle damage is similar; the black triangle behind the head distinguishes this one.
monitoring: Check seedlings daily in the first fortnight and pods weekly once they set.
prevention: Delay planting past the first spring generation. Row cover on seedlings. Clear crop debris where the adults overwinter.
organic_controls: Row cover on seedlings; hand-picking; neem on a light population. An established planting rarely needs anything at all.
chemical_controls: Pyrethrins and permethrin are registered. Treatment is usually only warranted on seedlings or when pods are being scarred; evening applications, as beans are bee-visited.
beneficials: Ground beetles, spiders, and a tachinid parasitoid of the adults.
treatments: Row cover the seedlings and otherwise tolerate it; treat only if pods are being scarred.

name: Japanese beetle
description: A metallic green and copper beetle about a centimetre long with white tufts along its sides. The adults feed in groups in full sun; the grubs live in lawn and pasture soil and eat grass roots.
signs: Leaves skeletonised between the veins into a lace, worst on the sunny top of the plant. Beetles clustered several to a leaf, since feeding damage releases a scent that draws more.
consequence: Ugly and sometimes severe defoliation, but established vegetables usually crop anyway. Basil and young beans suffer most.
look_alikes: Several native chafers are similar; the white side tufts are diagnostic.
monitoring: Walk the garden in the warmest part of a sunny day, when they are most active and most visible.
prevention: Do not hang pheromone traps in the garden: they attract far more beetles than they catch and reliably make the problem worse -- if a neighbour wants to hang one, downwind and a long way off. Keep plants watered so they grow through the damage.
organic_controls: Knock them into a jar of soapy water in the cool of early morning, when they are slow and drop rather than fly. Row cover over a small, badly hit crop such as basil. Neem is a mild deterrent rather than a kill.
chemical_controls: Carbaryl and pyrethroids are registered and are effective, and both are highly toxic to bees on crops that are flowering. For a garden the hand-picking is usually the better trade.
beneficials: Milky spore and parasitic nematodes act on the grubs in turf, but only over years and only over a large area; tachinid flies attack the adults.
treatments: Knock them into soapy water at dawn; row cover a favourite crop; never hang a pheromone trap in your own garden.

name: Stink bugs
latin_name: Halyomorpha halys; Chinavia hilaris; Euschistus servus
also_called: Brown marmorated stink bug; green stink bug
description: Shield-shaped true bugs that push a needle-like mouthpart into fruit and pods and drink. The damage is done in the moment of feeding and does not spread, but it does not heal either.
signs: Cloudy white or yellow spots just under the tomato skin, corky and hard when cut. Dimpled, deformed peppers. Pods that fail to fill. A strong smell when the bug is handled.
consequence: Fruit is edible but marked and often mealy where fed on. Feeding wounds are also where fruit rots begin.
look_alikes: Squash bugs are narrower and are on cucurbits. Several native stink bugs are predators of caterpillars and are worth leaving; a predatory species has a thickened, spined shoulder and is usually found on a caterpillar rather than a fruit.
monitoring: Check fruit and the tops of plants in the morning. Populations move in from field edges and weedy margins in late summer.
prevention: Keep the garden edges mown and free of the weedy hosts they build up on. Row cover on a small planting. A trap crop of sunflower or sorghum draws them off the tomatoes.
organic_controls: Hand-picking into soapy water, which is easiest early in the morning. Kaolin clay deters feeding. Removing weedy margins in late summer takes the reservoir away.
chemical_controls: Pyrethrins and permethrin are registered and give short-lived control at best -- these are strong fliers and the bed is recolonised within days. Hand-picking and margins are the better use of the effort. Any spray on a flowering crop goes on in the evening.
beneficials: Samurai wasp and other egg parasitoids, assassin bugs, spiders, birds.
treatments: Hand-pick in the morning; kaolin clay; mow the weedy margins; expect sprays to be short-lived.

name: Leaf-footed bugs
description: Large brown true bugs, 20 mm or so, with a white band across the back and flattened leaf-like flares on the hind legs. The nymphs are bright orange and cluster together, which is when they are easiest to deal with.
signs: Sunken, discoloured spots on tomatoes that stay hard. Shrivelled seeds in southern pea pods. Clusters of orange nymphs on a fruit truss.
consequence: Marked and mealy fruit rather than lost plants, and badly shrivelled peas. Numbers build sharply through late summer and autumn.
look_alikes: Wheel bugs and assassin bugs are predators and look superficially similar; leaf-footed bugs are the ones with the flared hind legs.
monitoring: Look for the orange nymph clusters from midsummer -- they are conspicuous and a whole cluster can be dealt with in one go.
prevention: Clear weedy hosts, especially thistle and sunflower, from the garden edges. Remove overwintering shelter such as woodpiles near the beds. Row cover on a small planting.
organic_controls: Hand-pick the nymph clusters into soapy water. A hand vacuum works well on adults. Insecticidal soap kills nymphs and does very little to adults.
chemical_controls: Pyrethrins as a last resort on the nymph stage; adults are hard to kill and quickly replaced. Evening applications on flowering crops.
beneficials: Tachinid flies, egg parasitoids, assassin bugs, birds.
treatments: Catch the orange nymph clusters early; hand-pick or vacuum adults; clear the weedy margins.

name: Harlequin bug
description: A boldly marked black-and-orange shield bug that feeds almost exclusively on brassicas. The barrel-shaped eggs are laid in neat double rows and look like tiny white kegs with black hoops.
signs: Pale blotches and white stippling on brassica leaves that turn brown and wilt. Whole plants collapsing in warm weather. The distinctive black-and-orange bugs are impossible to miss.
consequence: Young brassica plants are killed. An autumn planting can be lost entirely where the population has built up over summer.
look_alikes: Nothing else looks like it on a brassica.
monitoring: Check brassicas twice a week from planting, looking for the barrel-shaped egg rows on leaf undersides.
prevention: Row cover on brassicas from planting. Remove all brassica residue and wild mustard around the garden, which is where the population overwinters and builds. A trap crop of mustard planted early draws them off the main crop.
organic_controls: Hand-picking the adults and crushing the egg rows, done consistently, is effective. Insecticidal soap on the nymphs. A mustard trap crop, destroyed once colonised.
chemical_controls: Pyrethrins and permethrin are registered and work best on nymphs. Adults are hard to hit and often simply move.
beneficials: Egg parasitoids, though rarely enough on their own.
treatments: Row cover; crush the barrel-shaped egg rows; a mustard trap crop; clear wild mustard and old brassica stumps.

name: Leafminers
description: The larvae of small flies that live between the two surfaces of a leaf, eating a widening tunnel as they go. Nothing on the outside of the leaf ever touches them, which is why sprays disappoint.
signs: Pale winding tunnels or irregular blotches inside the leaf, wider at one end. Rows of white puncture dots along a leaf where the female fed.
consequence: Cosmetic on tomato and bean; on spinach, chard and beet, where the leaf is the crop, a mined leaf is not worth eating.
look_alikes: The tunnels are unmistakable. Do not confuse the feeding punctures with thrips stippling.
monitoring: Check leafy crops weekly. The first mines appear on older leaves; act before it reaches the crop leaves.
prevention: Floating row cover over spinach, chard and beet from sowing, which excludes the adult flies entirely and is the only reliable control. Remove and bag mined leaves as they appear. Clear crop residue.
organic_controls: Pick off and bin mined leaves -- squashing the larva in the mine between finger and thumb also works. Row cover. Spinosad has some translaminar movement into the leaf and is the only foliar spray worth trying.
chemical_controls: Most contact insecticides do nothing because the larva is inside the leaf, and they reliably kill the parasitic wasps that are the main natural control, making the next generation worse. Spinosad is the exception, and it is acutely toxic to bees while wet, so it goes on at dusk and not on anything in flower. This is a pest where spraying usually makes things worse.
beneficials: Diglyphus and Dacnusa parasitic wasps, which do most of the real control in an unsprayed garden.
treatments: Row cover on leafy crops; pick and bin mined leaves; do not spray a contact insecticide -- it removes the wasps and not the miners.

name: Slugs and snails
description: Molluscs that feed at night and in wet weather and shelter by day under boards, pots, mulch and leaf litter. They rasp holes in leaves and can shear a seedling off entirely.
signs: Irregular holes with smooth, rounded edges, often in the middle of a leaf. Silvery dried slime trails on leaves and soil in the morning. Seedlings gone overnight with nothing left.
consequence: Whole beds of seedlings lost in a wet spring, and hollowed strawberries and lettuce hearts later. The worst damage always happens in the week nobody was looking.
look_alikes: Earwig damage is similar but has no slime. Flea beetle holes are small and round; slug holes are large and irregular.
monitoring: Go out an hour after dark with a torch, which is the only time you will see the population honestly. Lay a board on damp soil and turn it each morning.
prevention: Water in the morning rather than the evening so the surface is dry at nightfall. Keep mulch a hand's width back from the stems of vulnerable plants. Clear boards, pots and debris from around the beds. A copper strip around a raised bed or a pot works while it stays clean.
organic_controls: Hand-collecting after dark, which is the most effective control there is. Board traps. Iron phosphate baits, which are approved for organic growing and are far safer around pets and wildlife than the older alternative. Beer traps catch some, and also attract more than they catch, so site them away from the crop.
chemical_controls: Iron phosphate is the bait to use. Metaldehyde baits are effective and are also acutely poisonous to dogs and cats -- do not use them where an animal or a child can reach the pellets.
beneficials: Ground beetles, toads, birds, and slow-worms where they occur. A garden that keeps its ground beetles has far fewer slugs.
treatments: Collect after dark with a torch; board traps; iron phosphate bait; water in the morning and keep mulch off the stems.

name: Earwigs
description: Brown insects with pincers at the tail, active at night and hiding in tight dark places by day. They eat aphids, mites and insect eggs as well as seedlings and soft fruit, so they are on both sides of the ledger.
signs: Ragged holes in soft leaves and flower petals, no slime. Earwigs found inside a corn husk, a strawberry or a rolled leaf during the day.
consequence: Mostly cosmetic and often outweighed by the aphids they eat. Real damage is limited to seedlings, soft fruit and sweet corn silk.
look_alikes: Slug damage has slime; caterpillar damage comes with frass.
monitoring: Roll a damp newspaper or lay a length of hose in the bed overnight and shake it out in the morning -- that is the population count and the trap in one.
prevention: Clear damp debris, boards and dense mulch next to vulnerable seedlings. Decide first whether they are doing net harm: in a garden with aphids, often not.
organic_controls: Rolled newspaper or hose traps, emptied each morning. Oil-and-soy-sauce traps sunk to soil level. A ring of diatomaceous earth around seedlings, renewed after rain.
chemical_controls: Baits containing spinosad are registered. Treatment is rarely justified: this is an animal worth tolerating unless it is actually eating the crop.
beneficials: They are one themselves -- earwigs are significant predators of aphids and codling moth eggs.
treatments: Trap with rolled newspaper or a length of hose and empty it daily; clear damp debris beside seedlings; tolerate the rest.

name: Root maggots
description: Small white legless maggots, the larvae of flies that lay their eggs at the base of the stem in cool, moist spring weather. The maggots eat the roots and tunnel into the bulb or the taproot.
signs: A plant that wilts in the sun and does not recover, with a stunted blue-green cast. Radishes and turnips tunnelled with brown scars. Onion bulbs rotting from the base with maggots inside. Lift a failing plant and the roots are gone.
consequence: The plant dies and nothing can be done for it once the maggots are in. In a cool wet spring a whole row of brassica transplants or onion sets can go.
look_alikes: Wireworm tunnels are narrow and clean; root maggot damage is a rotten mess. Clubroot swells the roots instead of eating them.
monitoring: Watch spring transplants closely in cool damp weather. Lift the first plant that wilts and look, rather than watering it more.
prevention: This is a prevention-only pest. Floating row cover from the day of planting, sealed at the soil, excludes the fly and is the whole answer. A collar of card or roofing felt flat on the soil around the stem stops egg-laying at the base. Rotate brassicas and onions well away from last year. Delay planting past the first spring flight where it is known.
organic_controls: Row cover and stem collars. Parasitic nematodes drenched into the soil at planting help. Destroy affected plants and their roots rather than leaving them to complete the generation.
chemical_controls: There is no effective rescue treatment available to a home garden once the maggots are in the root. Soil drenches sold for the purpose are largely ineffective at that point, which is why every extension recommendation here is about exclusion.
beneficials: Ground beetles and rove beetles take the eggs and are worth protecting by not disturbing the soil surface unnecessarily.
treatments: Row cover from planting or a collar flat on the soil; rotate; there is no cure once the roots are eaten.

name: Carrot rust fly
description: A small dark fly whose larvae tunnel through carrot roots leaving rusty-brown trails. The adults fly low over the ground and find the crop by smell, which is why bruised foliage attracts them.
signs: Rusty brown tunnels just under the skin of a carrot, filled with crumbly frass. Foliage tinged red or bronze and stunted. Damage is usually worst at the end of a long season.
consequence: The roots are inedible where tunnelled and rot in storage. A late-lifted crop can be almost entirely spoiled.
look_alikes: Wireworm holes are round, clean and go straight in; rust fly tunnels wander and are rusty.
monitoring: Pull a test carrot every few weeks from late summer. There is no useful above-ground sign until the damage is done.
prevention: Insect mesh over the bed from sowing, or a vertical barrier 60 cm high around it -- the flies fly low and will not go over. Sow after the first spring flight and lift before the autumn generation matures. Thin in the evening and remove the thinnings, because the smell of crushed foliage is what draws the fly. Rotate away from last year's carrot ground.
organic_controls: Mesh, barriers and timing. Parasitic nematodes drenched on the bed give partial control. Resistant varieties exist and are worth seeking out.
chemical_controls: No effective home-garden rescue treatment: the larva is inside the root. Everything that works here is exclusion or timing.
beneficials: Ground beetles and rove beetles take eggs and pupae.
treatments: Mesh or a low barrier from sowing; thin in the evening and take the thinnings away; time the sowing and lift promptly.

name: Wireworms
description: The hard, shiny, orange-brown larvae of click beetles. They live in soil for two to five years and are far more numerous in ground that was recently in grass or pasture.
signs: Neat round holes bored straight into potatoes, carrots and beetroot. Seedlings and sown seed that simply fail, with the larva found in the soil at the seed.
consequence: Roots and tubers holed and unstorable, and gaps in a sown row. The population takes years to fall, so a bed broken out of lawn is a problem for several seasons.
look_alikes: Millipedes are round and coil up; wireworms are flat-bodied, hard and stiff. Millipedes usually enlarge damage that something else began.
monitoring: Bury a piece of potato or carrot on a stick every couple of metres a fortnight before planting and dig it up to count what has moved in. That is the only honest estimate.
prevention: Do not plant potatoes and root crops in the first year or two after breaking sod. Cultivate repeatedly through a fallow season, which exposes larvae to birds and dries them out. Lift potatoes as soon as they are ready rather than leaving them in the ground.
organic_controls: Bait trapping before planting, then removal. Repeated shallow cultivation. Parasitic nematodes help in a small bed. Choosing what to grow -- lettuce and brassicas suffer far less than potatoes -- is the practical answer for a new bed.
chemical_controls: Soil insecticides for wireworm are not available to home gardens in any useful form, and would not be worth it if they were. This is a rotation and timing problem.
beneficials: Birds, ground beetles, and moles, which is the one good thing about a mole.
treatments: Bait-trap before planting; keep potatoes and roots out of newly broken sod; cultivate and lift promptly.

name: Fire ants
description: Mound-building ants that sting painfully and defend the mound in numbers. They eat few plants directly but tend aphids and scale for their honeydew and drive off the predators that would otherwise control them.
signs: Loose crumbly mounds with no obvious entrance hole, appearing overnight after rain. Ants streaming up plant stems to aphid colonies. Stings on anyone weeding.
consequence: Chiefly a hazard to the gardener and a reason the aphids are not being eaten. Occasional direct damage to seedlings, okra buds and ripe fruit close to the ground.
look_alikes: Other mound-building ants are harmless; disturb a mound gently from a safe distance and fire ants boil out immediately and aggressively.
monitoring: Walk the beds after rain, when new mounds appear. Look for ant trails on any plant carrying aphids.
prevention: Nothing keeps them out of a garden in the areas they occupy. Keeping mounds out of the beds themselves is the achievable goal.
organic_controls: Repeated drenching of a mound with several litres of boiling water kills a good proportion and harms nothing else, though it also kills roots where it runs. Spinosad-based fire ant baits are approved for organic growing and are the practical control. Bait around the beds and not in them.
chemical_controls: Bait products carrying hydramethylnon, indoxacarb or spinosad are the effective option and work by being carried into the colony, so they are broadcast around the garden rather than mixed into the soil of a bed. Read the label for the distance to an edible crop, which differs by product.
beneficials: Phorid decapitating flies, released regionally, reduce foraging over years rather than seasons.
treatments: Bait around the beds rather than in them; boiling water on an individual mound; expect to keep doing it.

name: Damping off
description: Soil-borne fungi and water moulds that rot seedlings at or just below the soil line. It is a disease of the propagation bench far more than of the garden, and of cold wet soil, poor airflow and reused trays.
signs: Seed that never emerges. A seedling that topples with a thin, water-soaked, pinched stem at soil level while the top is still green. White fuzzy growth on the surface of the mix in bad cases.
consequence: The seedling dies and does not recover. A whole tray can go in two days, and it takes the sowing date with it -- which for a heat-loving crop can mean the season.
look_alikes: Cutworms sever a stem cleanly and leave the top lying beside it. Drying out wilts a seedling without the pinched, dark stem base.
monitoring: Look at trays daily in the first fortnight. One toppled seedling is the warning; the tray is decided in the next two days.
prevention: This is entirely a prevention problem. Use fresh sterile seed-starting mix, not garden soil and not last year opened bag. Wash and disinfect reused trays. Sow thinly. Bottom-water and let the surface dry between waterings. Keep air moving with a small fan. Do not sow into cold soil -- warm the mix to the seed temperature range the research card gives.
organic_controls: Remove affected seedlings and the mix around them at once. A thin layer of coarse vermiculite or sand on the surface keeps the collar dry. Chamomile tea and cinnamon are traditional and unreliable; airflow and drier surfaces are what actually work. Biological drenches based on Trichoderma or Bacillus subtilis are registered and help as a preventive, not a cure.
chemical_controls: Fungicidal drenches are of very limited use once symptoms appear and are largely unavailable for home seed-starting. Seed treated with a fungicide by the supplier is the one chemical control that reliably matters, and it is bought rather than applied.
beneficials: Trichoderma and Bacillus subtilis in commercial biological drenches and in good compost.
treatments: Fresh sterile mix, clean trays, thin sowing, bottom watering and a fan. There is no cure -- everything here is prevention.

name: Early blight
description: A fungal leaf spot that overwinters on crop debris and in the soil and splashes up onto the lowest leaves in the first warm wet spell. It works steadily upward through the season.
signs: Brown spots on the lowest leaves with concentric rings inside them, like a target, and a yellow halo around each. Leaves yellow and drop from the bottom up. Dark sunken lesions with rings on the stem end of fruit.
consequence: Steady defoliation from the base up through the season, which cuts the crop and leaves the fruit exposed to sunscald. Rarely kills the plant outright but reliably shortens its useful life by weeks.
look_alikes: Septoria leaf spot makes smaller round spots with pale centres and black dots and no target rings. Late blight lesions are greasy and grey-green and spread far faster.
monitoring: Check the lowest leaves weekly from the moment fruit sets. The first target-ringed spot is the moment to act, not the moment to wait.
prevention: Mulch heavily under tomatoes so rain cannot splash soil onto leaves -- this is the single most effective measure. Stake or cage for airflow. Water at the base and in the morning, never over the leaves. Rotate away from tomato and potato ground for two or three years. Remove the lowest leaves up to the first flower cluster. Choose varieties listed as tolerant.
organic_controls: Remove and bag affected lower leaves as they appear; do not compost them. Copper and Bacillus subtilis fungicides give useful protection when started before the disease is established and repeated. Nothing cures an infected leaf.
chemical_controls: Copper-based fungicides and chlorothalonil are the garden actives, and both are protectants -- they stop new infection and do nothing for the spots already there, so they must go on early and be repeated after rain. Copper accumulates in soil with repeated use.
beneficials: Bacillus subtilis biofungicides.
treatments: Mulch, airflow, water at the base, strip the lowest leaves, rotate; copper or Bacillus subtilis early and repeated.

name: Late blight
description: The disease of the Irish potato famine, and still the most destructive thing that can happen to a tomato. It is a water mould, not a true fungus, it needs cool wet weather, and it can destroy a planting in under a week.
signs: Greasy grey-green blotches on leaves that turn brown-black, often starting at the leaf tip or edge. White fuzzy growth on the underside in humid mornings. Firm brown greasy patches on green fruit. A distinct smell of rot.
consequence: Total loss of tomatoes and potatoes, fast. It also spreads on the wind to every garden downwind, which makes destroying an infected plant a neighbourly act rather than only a personal one.
look_alikes: Early blight has concentric rings and moves slowly. Late blight is greasy, spreads in days, and shows white sporulation on leaf undersides in the morning.
monitoring: In cool wet weather check daily. Late blight forecasts are published regionally; if it is reported nearby, treat that as a warning to act.
prevention: Buy certified disease-free seed potatoes and healthy transplants. Never leave cull potatoes or volunteers over winter, which is where it survives. Airflow, staking and morning watering at the base. Resistant varieties exist and are the best defence in areas where it recurs.
organic_controls: Pull and bag infected plants immediately -- do not compost them, and do not leave them on the ground. Copper fungicides applied preventively during cool wet spells slow it. Once it is established in a planting, removal is the only responsible action.
chemical_controls: Copper and chlorothalonil are the garden protectants and must be on the plant before infection. There is no home-garden curative for late blight.
beneficials: None of practical use.
treatments: Resistant varieties and clean seed; copper preventively in cool wet weather; pull and bag infected plants at once.

name: Septoria leaf spot
description: A fungal leaf spot of tomatoes that overwinters on debris and on solanaceous weeds and comes up onto the lower leaves with splashing rain. It is often mistaken for early blight and treated the same way, which is fortunate because the treatment is the same.
signs: Many small round spots, three or four millimetres, with grey or tan centres and dark borders, on the lower leaves first. Tiny black dots visible in the centres with a hand lens. Leaves yellow and drop rapidly.
consequence: Rapid defoliation from the bottom up, which cuts yield and sunscalds the fruit. The fruit itself is not spotted, which is the difference from early blight.
look_alikes: Early blight spots are larger, fewer and have concentric rings. Bacterial spot lesions are darker and more angular and reach the fruit.
monitoring: Inspect the lowest leaves weekly from first fruit set, especially after rain.
prevention: Mulch to stop soil splash. Space and stake for airflow. Water at the base in the morning. Remove the lowest leaves. Rotate. Clear all tomato debris and nightshade weeds at the end of the season, since that is where it overwinters.
organic_controls: Remove and bag spotted leaves early and often. Copper or Bacillus subtilis as a protectant, started before the disease has climbed the plant.
chemical_controls: Copper and chlorothalonil, applied as protectants and repeated after rain. Neither cures an existing spot.
beneficials: Bacillus subtilis biofungicides.
treatments: Mulch, airflow and base watering; strip and bag spotted lower leaves; copper or Bacillus subtilis early.

name: Powdery mildew
description: A fungus that grows on the leaf surface rather than inside it, which is why it can be treated when almost nothing else can. Unusually among fungal diseases it does not need leaf wetness -- warm days, cool nights and humidity are enough.
signs: Round white powdery patches on the upper leaf surface first, spreading until whole leaves are coated, then yellow and brown. Cucurbits are the usual victims and are hit late in the season.
consequence: Loses the plant its leaves in the last month of cropping, which reduces the final picking and, on winter squash, the sugar and the storage life of what is already set.
look_alikes: Downy mildew makes angular yellow patches bounded by leaf veins, with grey fuzz on the UNDERSIDE. Powdery mildew is white, powdery and on top. Some squash varieties have natural silver leaf mottling that is easily mistaken for it -- rub it: mildew rubs off, mottling does not.
monitoring: From midsummer check the older, shadier leaves in the middle of the plant weekly. The first patch is usually low down and out of sight.
prevention: Choose resistant varieties, which for cucurbits are widely available and are much the best answer. Full sun and wide spacing. Avoid heavy nitrogen late. Remove the oldest leaves to open the canopy.
organic_controls: Because it lives on the surface, it can genuinely be treated: potassium bicarbonate, horticultural oils, and Bacillus subtilis all work if started at the first patch. Milk diluted in water has repeatedly shown real effect in trials. Remove and bag the worst leaves.
chemical_controls: Sulfur is the classic and effective active, and must not be applied above about 30C or within two weeks of an oil spray -- both burn the foliage. Potassium bicarbonate, neem oil and myclobutanil are also registered for gardens.
beneficials: Ampelomyces quisqualis, a fungus that parasitises mildew, occurs naturally and is sold as a biofungicide.
treatments: Resistant varieties and airflow; potassium bicarbonate, oil or sulfur at the first patch -- but never sulfur in heat or near an oil spray.

name: Downy mildew
description: A water mould, not a true fungus, that needs cool nights and leaf wetness. Cucurbit downy mildew does not overwinter in most of the country and blows north each summer, which is why regional forecasts can tell you the week it will arrive.
signs: Angular yellow patches on the upper leaf surface, sharply bounded by the veins so they look square-edged. Grey or purple fuzz on the underside in humid mornings. Whole leaves brown and die while the stems stay green.
consequence: On cucumbers and basil it kills the planting outright, often in ten days. Basil downy mildew makes the crop unusable and is now the main reason basil fails in a wet summer.
look_alikes: Powdery mildew is white and on the upper surface and rubs off. Angular leaf spot makes similar vein-bounded patches but they go papery and tear out.
monitoring: Follow the regional cucurbit downy mildew forecast where one is published, and check leaf undersides at first light in humid weather. On basil, check the undersides of the lower leaves before the yellowing shows.
prevention: Resistant varieties, which now exist for cucumber and for basil and are the only durable answer. Wide spacing and full sun. Water at the base in the morning. Plant early to crop before the annual arrival.
organic_controls: Copper fungicides applied preventively, starting when the disease is reported in the region rather than when it is seen. Remove and bag affected leaves. On basil, harvest hard and early and accept a shorter season.
chemical_controls: Copper and chlorothalonil are the garden protectants and must be on before infection; there is no curative for a home garden. Resistance to some actives is widespread in the cucurbit species.
beneficials: None of practical use.
treatments: Resistant varieties, spacing and morning base watering; copper preventively when it is reported in your area; bag affected leaves.

name: Bacterial wilt
description: A bacterium carried in the gut of striped and spotted cucumber beetles and introduced when they feed. It multiplies in the plants water-conducting tissue and blocks it. Cucumbers and muskmelons are highly susceptible; watermelon is largely immune.
signs: One runner wilts in the heat and recovers overnight, then does not. The whole vine follows within days while the leaves are still green. The test: cut a wilted stem, press the cut faces together and pull them slowly apart -- a fine white thread stretching between them is the bacterium.
consequence: The plant dies. There is no treatment at any stage, and the only control is not to let the beetles feed in the first place.
look_alikes: Squash vine borer leaves frass and a hole at the stem base. Fusarium wilt yellows one side of the plant first and stains the stem interior brown. Drought wilts at midday and recovers every evening.
monitoring: There is nothing to monitor for the disease itself -- monitor the beetles, from emergence, daily, on seedlings.
prevention: Everything is beetle control. Row cover from sowing until the first female flowers. Grow watermelon and Cucurbita moschata types where wilt is a recurring problem. Kaolin clay on young plants. Remove wilting plants at once so they are not a reservoir the beetles feed on.
organic_controls: Row cover, hand-picking beetles, kaolin clay, and prompt removal of infected plants. Nothing acts on the bacterium.
chemical_controls: No chemical treats the disease. Insecticides are aimed at the beetles and are covered under that entry, with the same warning: cucurbits depend on bees, so evenings only.
beneficials: Anything that eats cucumber beetles.
treatments: Prevent the beetles: row cover to first flower, kaolin clay, hand-picking. Pull wilting plants the day you see them.

name: Fusarium wilt
description: A soil fungus that enters through the roots and plugs the water-conducting tissue. It is host-specific -- the strain that kills tomatoes leaves melons alone -- and it survives in soil for many years, which makes it a decision about what to plant rather than something to treat.
signs: Yellowing and wilting that starts on one side of the plant or one branch, often with one side of a leaf yellow and the other green. Lower leaves first. Cut the stem lengthways near the base: a chocolate-brown stain in the ring just under the skin is the diagnosis.
consequence: The plant declines and dies, usually just as it begins to crop, and the ground stays infested for years afterwards.
look_alikes: Verticillium wilt looks almost identical and is distinguished mostly by cooler weather and a wider host range. Bacterial wilt of cucurbits gives the white thread test. Waterlogging wilts without staining the stem.
monitoring: Nothing useful before symptoms. Note where it happened, because that is the information that matters next year.
prevention: Resistant varieties are the whole answer and are widely available -- the F, FF or FFF on a tomato variety description is exactly this. Rotate for at least four years. Raise soil pH slightly and avoid excess nitrogen. Grafted tomatoes on resistant rootstock work where the ground is known to be infested. Solarising a bed under clear plastic through a hot summer reduces it.
organic_controls: Remove and bag affected plants with as much root as will come. Grow in containers or a raised bed with clean soil where a bed is known infested. Soil solarisation.
chemical_controls: No fungicide available to a home garden controls Fusarium wilt. Every recommendation here is variety choice, rotation and soil.
beneficials: Suppressive composts and Trichoderma biologicals reduce severity; they do not cure it.
treatments: Resistant varieties, long rotation, clean containers; there is no cure and the soil stays infested.

name: Verticillium wilt
description: A soil fungus much like Fusarium in what it does, but with a very wide host range and a preference for cooler soils. It persists in soil for a decade or more as resting structures.
signs: Yellowing in a V-shaped wedge from the leaf edge inward, lower leaves first. Wilting in the heat of the day, recovering at night, until it does not. A tan discoloration in the stem ring near the base, usually paler than the Fusarium stain.
consequence: Progressive decline and death, and ground that is unsuitable for the whole susceptible group for years.
look_alikes: Fusarium wilt, closely. The practical difference is that Verticillium hits a much broader range of plants and prefers cooler weather.
monitoring: Nothing before symptoms; record where it occurred.
prevention: Resistant varieties -- the V in a tomato variety description. A four-year rotation with grasses and sweet corn, which are not hosts. Avoid following strawberries, potatoes or brassica-free weedy ground with a susceptible crop. Solarisation helps.
organic_controls: Remove and bag affected plants. Grow susceptible crops in containers of clean mix on infested ground. Solarise the bed through a hot summer.
chemical_controls: No home-garden fungicide controls it.
beneficials: Broccoli residue incorporated into soil measurably suppresses Verticillium and is one of the few cultural tricks with real evidence behind it.
treatments: Resistant varieties and a long rotation through corn and grasses; containers on infested ground; no cure.

name: Southern blight
also_called: White mould of the stem base
description: A hot-weather soil fungus of the southern states that attacks the stem right at the soil line. It produces coarse white mycelium and small round tan sclerotia that look exactly like mustard seed, which is the diagnostic sign.
signs: Sudden wilt of an otherwise healthy plant in hot humid weather. A white fan of coarse fungal threads on the stem at soil level and on the soil around it, carrying tan or brown spheres the size of mustard seed.
consequence: The plant dies within days and the sclerotia stay in the soil for years. In a hot wet summer it can take several plants in a row.
look_alikes: White mould (Sclerotinia) makes larger, irregular black sclerotia inside the stem, and prefers cool weather. Southern blight is a heat disease and the sclerotia are outside, small, round and uniform.
monitoring: Look at the stem base of wilting plants in hot humid weather rather than assuming drought.
prevention: Deep burial of crop residue -- the fungus is aerobic and lives in the top few centimetres. Rotate to corn and small grains. Keep mulch and soil pulled back from the stem base. Solarisation reduces sclerotia in the top layer.
organic_controls: Remove the plant with a generous margin of soil and bag it. A collar of aluminium foil around the stem base protects a valued plant. Deep cultivation to bury the residue and the sclerotia.
chemical_controls: No effective home-garden fungicide. This is a residue, rotation and soil-management problem.
beneficials: Trichoderma biologicals give partial suppression.
treatments: Bury residue deeply, rotate to corn, keep mulch off the stem base; remove infected plants with their soil.

name: White mould
description: A cool-weather fungus that infects through dying flowers and wounds and rots stems from the inside. Hard black bodies the size and shape of rat droppings form inside the stem and fall into the soil, where they last for years.
signs: A water-soaked patch on a stem that goes white and cottony. Sudden collapse of a branch or a whole plant above that point. Split the stem and there are hard black lumps inside.
consequence: Loss of the plant or a major branch, and long-lived contamination of the bed. Beans and lettuce are the usual victims.
look_alikes: Southern blight is a heat disease with small tan sclerotia on the OUTSIDE of the stem at soil level. Grey mould is fuzzy and grey-brown rather than white and cottony.
monitoring: Check bean and lettuce stems in cool damp weather, especially where the canopy is dense and slow to dry.
prevention: Wide spacing and good airflow, which matters more here than almost anywhere. Avoid overhead watering. Rotate to corn and small grains, which are not hosts. Do not compost infected material. Avoid dense plantings on ground that has had it before.
organic_controls: Remove and bag infected plants including the sclerotia, cutting well below the lesion. Coniothyrium minitans, a fungus that parasitises the sclerotia, is sold as a soil biological and genuinely reduces the population over seasons.
chemical_controls: No reliable home-garden fungicide once it is established. Everything effective is spacing, airflow and rotation.
beneficials: Coniothyrium minitans.
treatments: Space widely, water at the base, rotate to corn; cut out and bag infected stems with the black bodies inside.

name: Grey mould
description: A fungus that lives on dead and dying tissue and moves from there into healthy tissue. Cool, damp, still air is what it needs, which makes it a greenhouse and a wet-spring disease.
signs: Fuzzy grey-brown mould on dead flowers, fruit and leaf tips. Pale ghost rings on green tomatoes where a spore landed and did not get in. Fruit rotting where it touches soil or another fruit.
consequence: Rotted fruit and lost flowers rather than lost plants, though a stem lesion can kill a branch. Mostly a wet-weather and under-cover problem.
look_alikes: White mould is white and cottony with black lumps inside the stem. Grey mould is dusty grey-brown and always starts on something already dead or dying.
monitoring: Look at spent flowers and any fruit touching the ground, weekly in damp weather.
prevention: Pick off dead flowers and leaves, which is what it feeds on before it feeds on the crop. Airflow, spacing, and no overhead watering. Under cover, ventilate rather than heat. Keep fruit off the soil with mulch or a support.
organic_controls: Sanitation is most of it: remove dead tissue and rotting fruit promptly and bag them. Bacillus subtilis biofungicides help preventively. Increase ventilation before reaching for anything.
chemical_controls: Bacillus subtilis and captan are registered for garden use. Botrytis develops fungicide resistance readily, so rotation of actives matters and sanitation matters more.
beneficials: Bacillus subtilis and Trichoderma biofungicides.
treatments: Remove dead flowers, leaves and rotting fruit; ventilate and space; Bacillus subtilis preventively in damp weather.

name: Anthracnose
description: A fungal fruit and leaf rot that overwinters on debris and in seed and spreads by rain splash in warm wet weather. It infects green fruit silently and only shows as the fruit ripens.
signs: Round sunken spots on ripe fruit, darkening in the middle with concentric rings of tiny dark dots, often with a pink or salmon slime in the centre in humid weather. On beans, dark sunken lesions on pods with pink centres.
consequence: Ripe tomatoes and peppers rot on the plant or in the bowl a day after picking. On beans it can also kill seedlings from infected seed.
look_alikes: Blossom end rot is on the bottom of the fruit only, dry, leathery and never has rings or spore masses.
monitoring: Watch ripening fruit in warm wet spells. Picking slightly early and ripening indoors avoids much of it.
prevention: Mulch to stop soil splash. Stake and space for airflow. Pick fruit promptly and never leave over-ripe fruit on the plant. Rotate for two or three years. Use clean, treated bean seed and never save seed from an affected crop. Do not work among wet bean plants -- that is how it spreads down a row.
organic_controls: Remove and bag affected fruit at once. Copper fungicides preventively in warm wet weather. Pick at first blush and finish ripening indoors.
chemical_controls: Copper and chlorothalonil as protectants, started before symptoms and repeated after rain.
beneficials: None of practical use.
treatments: Mulch, airflow and prompt picking; copper preventively in warm wet weather; bag affected fruit.

name: Bacterial spot and speck
latin_name: Xanthomonas spp.; Pseudomonas syringae pv. tomato
description: Bacterial diseases spread by rain splash, overhead water and handling wet plants, and carried on seed and transplants. Spot likes heat, speck likes cool weather, and the management is the same for both.
signs: Small dark angular leaf spots, often with a yellow halo, that dry and tear out leaving ragged holes. Raised scabby specks on the fruit that make it unmarketable. Heavy leaf drop.
