consequence: Defoliation and fruit that is edible but scabbed and unsellable. Once it is established in warm wet weather there is no way to stop it in a garden.
look_alikes: Septoria and early blight are fungal, round rather than angular, and do not scab the fruit. Bacterial spots are angular because they are bounded by the small veins.
monitoring: Look for angular spots after a run of wet weather, and check bought transplants before planting -- infected transplants are the commonest way it arrives.
prevention: Buy clean transplants and look at them. Use certified or hot-water-treated seed. Do not work among wet plants. Water at the base. Rotate for two years and remove all debris. Copper preventively where it recurs.
organic_controls: Remove badly affected leaves early. Copper, with or without a Bacillus subtilis product, applied preventively. Sanitation between plants when pruning -- a bacterial disease travels on hands and secateurs.
chemical_controls: Copper is the only garden active with real effect, it is protectant only, and copper-tolerant strains are now common. There is no cure.
beneficials: None of practical use.
treatments: Clean seed and clean transplants; never handle wet plants; base watering; copper preventively.

name: Angular leaf spot
description: A bacterial disease of cucurbits spread by splashing water, by cucumber beetles, and by hands and tools on wet foliage. It is seed-borne, which is why it appears in a garden that never had it.
signs: Water-soaked angular spots bounded by the leaf veins, drying tan and then falling out to leave ragged holes. Milky bacterial ooze on the underside in humid mornings, drying to a white crust. Small round water-soaked spots on the fruit.
consequence: Leaf loss and holed leaves; fruit spots let in the soft rots that follow. Not usually fatal but it shortens the picking.
look_alikes: Downy mildew is also vein-bounded but is yellow rather than water-soaked and has grey fuzz beneath. Angular leaf spot tears out and leaves holes; downy mildew does not.
monitoring: Look at leaf undersides in the morning after wet weather for the milky ooze, which is diagnostic.
prevention: Buy clean seed and do not save seed from an affected crop. Never work among wet vines. Water at the base. Rotate for two years and remove debris. Control cucumber beetles, which carry it.
organic_controls: Copper preventively. Sanitation, staying out of the wet crop, and removing the worst leaves.
chemical_controls: Copper, as a protectant. Nothing cures a bacterial leaf spot.
beneficials: None of practical use.
treatments: Clean seed, base watering, stay out of wet vines, rotate; copper preventively.

name: Black rot of brassicas
description: The most serious bacterial disease of brassicas worldwide. It enters through the pores at the leaf margin or through insect and hail wounds, moves into the veins, and works down to the stem.
signs: Yellow V-shaped wedges at the leaf margins, pointing inward, with blackened veins running through them. Cut the stem across and the vascular ring is black. Whole plants yellow, stunt and collapse.
consequence: Plants are lost and the seed and soil stay contaminated. In warm wet weather a whole brassica bed can go.
look_alikes: Fusarium yellows also yellows brassicas but does not blacken the veins or make a V at the margin. Nitrogen deficiency yellows the oldest leaves evenly and uniformly.
monitoring: Look at leaf margins weekly in warm wet weather. Inspect bought transplants -- this arrives on transplants and seed far more often than from the soil.
prevention: Hot-water-treated or certified seed. Buy clean transplants and reject any with yellow margins. Three-year rotation away from all brassicas, including weedy mustards. Do not work in the crop when wet. Wide spacing and base watering.
organic_controls: Remove and bag affected plants completely. Rotation and clean seed. Copper gives some protection early and cannot stop an established infection.
chemical_controls: Copper as a protectant only. There is no curative treatment.
beneficials: None of practical use.
treatments: Clean seed and transplants; three-year rotation; stay out of the wet crop; remove and bag affected plants.

name: Clubroot
description: A soil organism that infects brassica roots and makes them swell into distorted clubs that cannot take up water. Resting spores survive in soil for up to twenty years, and acid soils make it far worse.
signs: Wilting in the sun that recovers overnight, then stunting and yellowing. Lift the plant: the roots are swollen, knobbly and club-shaped rather than fibrous, and later rot into a foul mess.
consequence: The crop is lost and the ground is unusable for brassicas for many years. This is the one soil disease worth going to real lengths to keep out.
look_alikes: Root-knot nematode makes small beaded galls along fine roots; clubroot makes large distorted clubs on the main roots. Root maggots eat the roots away rather than swelling them.
monitoring: Lift and look at the roots of any stunted brassica rather than guessing. Knowing you have it changes the plan for a decade.
prevention: Never bring in soil, transplants or tools from an affected garden -- that is how it arrives. Lime to raise soil pH to about 7.2, which strongly suppresses it. Long rotation, seven years or more, and control weedy mustards, which are hosts. Improve drainage. Resistant varieties exist.
organic_controls: Liming, drainage and rotation. Grow brassicas in containers of clean mix where a bed is known infested. Remove and bag affected plants with their roots -- never compost them.
chemical_controls: No home-garden chemical controls it. Lime is the effective input and it is a soil amendment, not a fungicide.
beneficials: None of practical use.
treatments: Keep it out; lime to pH 7.2; long rotation and resistant varieties; containers on infested ground.

name: Root-knot nematodes
description: Microscopic roundworms that enter fine roots and cause the plant to grow galls around them. Worst in sandy soils and in long warm seasons, and they multiply on almost every summer vegetable.
signs: Plants stunted and wilting in the afternoon heat despite adequate water, yellowing and unresponsive to feeding, often in patches rather than across the whole bed. Lift a plant: the roots carry beaded swellings that cannot be rubbed off.
consequence: Reduced yield across the bed and progressively worse each year the same crops are grown. Carrots become forked and unusable.
look_alikes: The nitrogen-fixing nodules on bean and pea roots are also lumps -- but they rub off easily and are round and attached to the outside, while galls are part of the root itself. Clubroot makes large clubs on brassicas, which nematodes do not attack.
monitoring: Lift and examine roots at the end of every season in a bed that underperformed. That is the only reliable diagnosis and it is free.
prevention: Resistant varieties -- the N in a tomato variety code. Rotate to non-hosts: sweet corn, small grains, and resistant cover crops. Solarise the bed under clear plastic through the hottest six weeks of summer. Add organic matter, which supports the fungi and predators that keep numbers down. Grow susceptible crops in containers on badly infested ground.
organic_controls: Solarisation, rotation, resistant varieties, French marigold cover crops grown as a solid stand for a full season -- interplanting a few marigolds does nothing, and this is a very common misconception. Large additions of compost.
chemical_controls: Nematicides are not available to home gardens, and would not be a good idea if they were. Everything effective here is rotation, soil and variety choice.
beneficials: Nematode-trapping fungi and predatory mites, all favoured by high organic matter.
treatments: Resistant varieties, rotation to corn, solarisation, plenty of compost; a solid marigold cover crop, not a few plants dotted about.

name: Mosaic viruses
latin_name: Cucumber mosaic virus; Tobacco mosaic virus
description: A group of viruses spread mostly by aphids, and in the tobacco mosaic group also by hands, tools and tobacco products. Once a plant is infected it stays infected, and there is no treatment at any price.
signs: Mottled light and dark green patchwork on the leaves. Puckered, narrow, strap-like or fern-like new growth. Stunting. Mottled or bumpy fruit that fails to size.
consequence: A permanently reduced or worthless plant, and a reservoir for the aphids to move it on to the neighbours. Removal is the only useful response.
look_alikes: Herbicide drift also distorts new growth, usually across every plant in a direction rather than plant by plant. Nutrient deficiencies mottle without distorting.
monitoring: Look at the newest growth. A mottled, distorted growing point on one plant while its neighbours are normal is the pattern.
prevention: Control aphids early. Buy resistant varieties. Wash hands and disinfect tools between plants, and do not handle tomatoes after handling tobacco, which genuinely transmits TMV. Control perennial weeds that host the viruses. Reflective mulch deters incoming aphids.
organic_controls: Pull and bag infected plants as soon as you are confident, before the aphids move it on. Aphid control on the rest. Nothing treats an infected plant.
chemical_controls: None. No chemical affects a plant virus.
beneficials: Everything that eats aphids.
treatments: Resistant varieties, aphid control and clean hands; pull and bag infected plants -- there is no cure.

name: Curly top virus
description: A virus carried by the beet leafhopper, which blows in from dry rangeland in early summer. The leafhopper infects a plant in a single brief feed and moves on, so the damage is scattered rather than spreading plant to plant.
signs: A plant that stops dead: leaves thickened, stiff, crinkled and rolled upward, yellowing with purple veins. Fruit ripens prematurely and small. Individual plants scattered through an otherwise healthy bed.
consequence: The affected plant is finished and will not produce. Neighbouring plants are usually fine, because the vector does not stay.
look_alikes: Herbicide damage distorts growth across a whole area. Mosaic viruses mottle rather than stiffen and thicken. Curly top leaves feel leathery and brittle, which is quite distinctive to the hand.
monitoring: Nothing useful -- by the time it shows, the leafhopper is long gone. Note how many plants are affected and plan shade for next year.
prevention: Shade cloth or row cover over the crop in early summer, which deters the leafhopper, is the only measure with real effect. Plant densely so the leafhopper is less attracted to bare soil between plants. Control host weeds in the surroundings. Some pepper and bean varieties carry tolerance.
organic_controls: Remove infected plants -- more for tidiness than for control, since the vector is not resident. Shade and dense planting for the rest of the season.
chemical_controls: Insecticides do not help: the leafhopper transmits it in a feed shorter than any spray can prevent, and it does not colonise the crop.
beneficials: None of practical use.
treatments: Shade cloth or row cover in early summer, dense planting, tolerant varieties; pull affected plants -- nothing treats the virus.

name: Tomato spotted wilt virus
description: A virus that only thrips can transmit, and only if they acquired it as larvae. It has an enormous host range including many ornamentals and weeds, which is where it usually comes from.
signs: Bronzing and dark spots on young leaves, with the growing tip often dying back. Distinctive ringspots and concentric yellow or orange rings on the fruit as it ripens. Marked one-sided stunting.
consequence: The plant is finished; fruit already set is spotted and unusable. Removal is the only action.
look_alikes: The fruit ringspots are close to unique. Early leaf bronzing looks like spider mite damage, but there is no webbing and no mites.
monitoring: Watch for bronzed growing tips from early summer. Sticky cards for thrips give the earlier warning.
prevention: Resistant tomato and pepper varieties, carrying the Sw-5 gene, are the effective answer where the virus is common. Thrips control on young plants. Remove weedy hosts and any infected ornamental. Reflective mulch delays thrips arrival.
organic_controls: Pull and bag infected plants the day you are confident. Thrips control with spinosad at dusk on the remainder. Reflective mulch.
chemical_controls: Nothing treats the virus. Insecticides against thrips only reduce further spread, and imperfectly.
beneficials: Minute pirate bugs and predatory mites, against the thrips.
treatments: Resistant varieties, thrips control and reflective mulch; pull infected plants at once -- there is no cure.

name: Tomato yellow leaf curl virus
description: A whitefly-transmitted virus, spreading north through the warmer states. A whitefly that has fed on an infected plant carries it for the rest of its life.
signs: Severe upward cupping and curling of leaves with yellow margins, marked stunting with very short internodes so the plant looks bunched, and flowers that drop without setting fruit.
consequence: A plant infected young sets nothing at all. There is no treatment.
look_alikes: Herbicide drift, particularly from growth-regulator herbicides, curls and cups leaves similarly -- but affects everything nearby rather than scattered plants, and does not stunt the internodes the same way. Physiological leaf roll is smooth, thick and green and does not yellow.
monitoring: Whitefly monitoring with yellow sticky cards is the useful early signal. Check transplants before planting.
prevention: Resistant varieties, now widely sold where the virus is present, are the answer. Whitefly exclusion with fine mesh on young plants. Remove infected plants promptly, bagging them rather than shaking the whiteflies off. Do not plant near an old infected crop.
organic_controls: Bag the whole plant before pulling it so the whiteflies go with it. Whitefly control with soap and oil. Reflective mulch.
chemical_controls: Nothing treats the virus; whitefly control only slows the spread.
beneficials: Encarsia wasps and other whitefly parasitoids.
treatments: Resistant varieties and whitefly exclusion; bag infected plants before pulling them.

name: Rust
description: Fungi that produce powdery pustules of orange or brown spores on the leaf surface, favoured by long dew periods and moderate temperatures. Each host has its own rust and they do not cross over.
signs: Small raised rusty-orange pustules, mostly on leaf undersides, that rub off onto a finger. Later they darken to brown or black. Leaves yellow and drop.
consequence: Leaf loss late in the season that cuts the last of the crop. Rarely fatal but a heavy attack on beans ends the picking early.
look_alikes: Nothing else leaves orange powder on a finger. Do not confuse with the harmless orange spots of some leaf-mining flies.
monitoring: Check leaf undersides weekly from midsummer, especially in a spell of heavy dew.
prevention: Resistant varieties. Wide spacing and morning watering at the base so leaves dry quickly. Rotate. Remove and destroy crop residue, and on garlic and onion do not leave volunteers standing.
organic_controls: Remove affected leaves early. Sulfur applied at first sign is genuinely effective on rust, subject to the heat and oil warnings. Copper is less effective here than on the bacterial diseases.
chemical_controls: Sulfur, and myclobutanil among the synthetics. Never apply sulfur above about 30C or within two weeks of an oil spray.
beneficials: None of practical use.
treatments: Resistant varieties, airflow and base watering; sulfur at the first pustules, not in heat.

name: Tomato leaf mould
description: A fungal disease of high humidity, and overwhelmingly a greenhouse and tunnel problem rather than an outdoor one. It needs sustained humidity above about 85 per cent, which is what a closed tunnel provides every night.
signs: Pale green to yellow blotches on the upper leaf surface with no sharp edge, and olive-green to brown velvety mould on the underside directly beneath them. Lower leaves first.
consequence: Progressive defoliation under cover, cutting the crop badly in a tunnel or greenhouse. Outdoors it is usually minor.
look_alikes: Early blight and Septoria make defined spots. Leaf mould blotches are diffuse on top with velvet underneath, which is the giveaway.
monitoring: Under cover, look at the undersides of the lower leaves weekly from the first fruit set.
prevention: Ventilation, ventilation, ventilation -- vent overnight rather than closing up. Wide spacing, hard pruning of lower leaves, and no overhead watering. Resistant varieties are widely available and are the practical answer for a tunnel.
organic_controls: Increase airflow and remove affected leaves. Copper and Bacillus subtilis preventively.
chemical_controls: Copper and chlorothalonil as protectants. Managing the humidity does more than any spray.
beneficials: None of practical use.
treatments: Ventilate hard overnight, prune and space, resistant varieties; copper preventively under cover.

name: Cercospora leaf spot
description: A warm, humid-weather fungal leaf spot, most familiar on beetroot and chard, where it can strip a crop of usable leaves in a wet August.
signs: Small round spots with pale tan or grey centres and distinct reddish-purple borders. Centres often drop out leaving shot holes. Spots coalesce and leaves collapse.
consequence: On chard and beet greens, where the leaf is the crop, it ends the picking. On roots it reduces size rather than ruining them.
look_alikes: Bacterial leaf spot of beet is angular and water-soaked without the purple ring. The purple border is the useful sign.
monitoring: Check chard and beet weekly through warm humid weather.
prevention: Wide spacing and airflow. Base watering in the morning. Two-year rotation and removal of debris, where it overwinters. Pick outer leaves regularly, which both harvests and thins.
organic_controls: Strip and bag affected leaves, which on chard is also just harvesting. Copper preventively in a wet spell.
chemical_controls: Copper and chlorothalonil as protectants.
beneficials: None of practical use.
treatments: Space, water at the base, pick the outer leaves often, rotate; copper in a wet spell.

name: Aster yellows
description: A phytoplasma -- a bacterium without a cell wall -- carried by the aster leafhopper, which migrates north on spring winds. It affects an extremely wide range of plants and produces some of the strangest symptoms in the garden.
signs: Bizarre distorted growth: carrots with a mass of hairy roots and a red-purple bunched top; lettuce with twisted yellow inner leaves; flowers that come out green and leafy instead of coloured. Bitter, hairy carrots are the classic sign.
consequence: The affected plant is unusable. The carrots taste bitter and the tops are inedible.
look_alikes: Herbicide injury distorts too, but affects a whole area. The green, leafy flowers of aster yellows are close to unmistakable.
monitoring: Nothing useful before symptoms. Note the incidence and remove.
prevention: Control the perennial weeds that host it -- thistle, plantain, dandelion. Row cover over carrots and lettuce in early summer excludes the leafhoppers. Remove affected plants promptly so a leafhopper does not pick it up again.
organic_controls: Removal and weed control. Row cover during the leafhopper flight.
chemical_controls: Nothing treats a phytoplasma. Insecticides against leafhoppers are largely ineffective on a migrating vector.
beneficials: None of practical use.
treatments: Row cover in early summer, clear perennial broadleaf weeds, remove affected plants; there is no cure.

name: Corn smut
description: A fungus that infects corn through wounds and growing tissue and turns kernels into large silvery-grey galls full of black spores. It is also a delicacy in Mexican cooking, sold as huitlacoche and picked young and firm.
signs: Swollen silvery-white galls on ears, tassels or stalks, sometimes the size of a fist, that split and release a mass of powdery black spores.
consequence: The affected ear is lost as sweet corn. Spores persist in soil for years. Damage is usually to a few plants rather than a whole planting.
look_alikes: Nothing else looks like it.
monitoring: Walk the corn weekly from tasselling. Removing a gall before it bursts is the whole of the control.
prevention: Avoid injuring plants when cultivating or detasselling -- most infection is through wounds. Balanced nitrogen rather than excess. Rotate. Some varieties are more tolerant.
organic_controls: Cut out and bag galls while they are still firm and white, before they split. Do not compost them. Or pick them at that stage and cook them.
chemical_controls: No effective home-garden fungicide, and none is warranted.
beneficials: None of practical use.
treatments: Cut galls out while still white and firm and bag them, or eat them; avoid wounding the plants; rotate.

name: Onion neck rot and basal rot
latin_name: Botrytis allii; Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. cepae
description: Two storage rots with different causes and the same practical answer. Neck rot enters through the neck as the crop dies down and shows up in storage; basal rot comes up through the base plate from infested soil.
signs: In storage, a soft sunken area at the neck with grey mould between the scales, or a bulb rotting from the base upward with white fluff on the base plate. In the field, premature yellowing and a bulb that lifts away from its roots.
consequence: A crop that looked fine at lifting turns to mush over the winter. This is where most home-stored onions and garlic are lost.
look_alikes: Onion maggot damage has maggots in it. Simple bruising rots at the point of damage rather than from the neck or the base.
monitoring: Check stored bulbs monthly and remove any that softens; one rotting bulb spoils those around it.
prevention: Almost all of this is curing and storage. Lift when the tops have fallen, cure in a warm airy place until the necks are papery and tight, and store cool, dry and with air movement. Do not damage bulbs at lifting. Do not over-feed with nitrogen late, which makes thick soft necks. Rotate away from alliums for four years for basal rot.
organic_controls: Careful lifting, thorough curing, cool dry airy storage, and inspection. Discard any bulb with a thick soft neck rather than storing it.
chemical_controls: No useful home-garden treatment. This is a harvest and storage problem, and it is solved there.
beneficials: None of practical use.
treatments: Cure thoroughly until the necks are papery, store cool dry and airy, lift without bruising, rotate.

name: Blossom end rot
description: Not a disease and not a pest: a calcium supply failure in the fruit. Almost always the soil has plenty of calcium and the plant could not move it fast enough, because water uptake was uneven while the fruit was sizing.
signs: A sunken, leathery, dark brown or black patch on the BOTTOM of the fruit, opposite the stem. Dry and flat rather than mouldy, though moulds move in later. First fruits of the season are the usual victims.
consequence: The affected fruit is spoiled. The plant is fine and later fruit is usually normal once watering steadies, which is why this is a disorder and not a disease.
look_alikes: Anthracnose is on the side or the shoulder, is circular and sunken with rings, and often has pink spore masses. Sunscald is on the sun-facing side and is pale and papery.
monitoring: Watch the first fruits of each planting. If the first truss has it and the second does not, the watering has already been fixed.
prevention: Even, deep watering is the whole of it. Mulch to buffer the soil. Do not let a container dry out and then flood it -- containers are where this happens most. Avoid heavy nitrogen, especially ammonium forms, which competes with calcium uptake. Do not damage roots by cultivating close to the plant. Get a soil test before adding calcium at all.
organic_controls: Steady watering and mulch. Remove affected fruit so the plant puts its resources into the next ones.
chemical_controls: Calcium sprays and soil calcium additions are widely sold for this and rarely help, because the soil almost always has enough calcium already and a leaf spray does not reach the fruit. Fix the watering instead. Add lime or gypsum only if a soil test actually shows a calcium shortage or a pH problem.
treatments: Even deep watering and mulch. Calcium sprays are usually money for nothing -- the problem is water, not calcium.

name: Heat blossom drop
description: Flowers abort without setting when it is too hot, too cold, too dry or too windy at the moment of pollination. For tomatoes the classic trigger is night temperatures above about 24C or day temperatures above about 35C; pollen is simply not viable then.
signs: Flowers yellow at the stalk and drop off cleanly with no fruit behind them. The plant itself looks perfectly healthy and keeps producing more flowers.
consequence: A gap in the harvest six to eight weeks later, which is the part people notice. In a long hot summer this is why tomatoes stop and then start again in September.
look_alikes: Poor pollination in cucurbits drops small fruit that started to swell; heat blossom drop loses the flower before anything sets. Curly top and mosaic virus also stop fruit set but distort the plant as well.
monitoring: Note the nights above 24C -- Carl has the temperatures already. The blossom drop follows two or three days later.
prevention: Choose heat-set varieties where summers are long and hot; this is the only measure that really works. Shade cloth of 30 to 50 per cent over the hottest weeks. Keep the soil evenly moist so the plant is not also water-stressed. Plant early enough that the main set happens before the heat.
organic_controls: Shade cloth, steady water, and patience. The plant will set again when the nights cool, which is what a late-summer flush is.
chemical_controls: Blossom-set hormone sprays exist and give erratic results, often producing hollow or misshapen fruit. Not worth it.
treatments: Heat-set varieties, 30-50 per cent shade cloth over the worst weeks, steady water; it sets again when nights cool.

name: Fruit cracking
description: A fruit that has slowed its growth in a dry spell takes up water faster than its skin can stretch when the rain finally comes. Cabbages and carrots split for the same reason.
signs: Concentric rings of cracks around the shoulders of a tomato, or radial cracks running down from the stem. Splits in cabbage heads and carrot roots after heavy rain.
consequence: Cosmetic if picked at once. Left on the plant the cracks let in the rots and the fruit flies, and then it is a loss.
look_alikes: Catfacing is deformity from the flower stage, present from the start; cracking appears on a fruit that was smooth yesterday.
monitoring: Pick ripening fruit before forecast heavy rain. Carl has the forecast on the menu -- that is what it is for.
prevention: Even watering and heavy mulch to buffer the swing. Pick at first blush and ripen indoors in an unsettled week. Crack-resistant varieties exist and differ enormously. Do not over-water a cabbage that is nearly ready, and cut it rather than leaving it.
organic_controls: Pick promptly. Use the cracked ones first and cut the cracks out.
chemical_controls: None, and none needed.
treatments: Even watering and mulch; pick before heavy rain; choose crack-resistant varieties.

name: Sunscald
description: Fruit exposed to direct sun after the leaves that shaded it are lost -- to disease, to over-pruning, or to a hornworm -- is literally cooked on the sunny side.
signs: A pale white or yellow patch on the sun-facing side of the fruit that turns papery, sunken and thin. Secondary black moulds grow on the dead tissue afterwards.
consequence: The affected fruit is spoiled. It is a symptom as much as a problem: the real question is why the canopy went.
look_alikes: Blossom end rot is on the bottom and is dark and leathery. Anthracnose is circular and ringed and can be anywhere.
monitoring: After any defoliation event -- a blight outbreak, a hornworm, a hard prune -- look at what is now exposed.
prevention: Keep the canopy: control the leaf diseases and do not over-prune. Shade cloth over a plant that has lost its leaves. Do not strip leaves to hurry ripening, which is a common and counterproductive habit.
organic_controls: Shade cloth or a light cover over exposed fruit. Kaolin clay reflects heat and helps on a badly exposed plant.
chemical_controls: None. Treat the cause of the defoliation instead.
treatments: Keep the leaves on -- control the leaf disease, do not over-prune; shade cloth or kaolin on exposed fruit.

name: Catfacing
description: Deformity that happens at the flower stage, when cold weather, very hot weather, damage or heavy nitrogen disturb the developing flower. The fruit grows around the injury.
signs: Puckered, scarred, lobed or kidney-shaped fruit with corky brown bands and sometimes holes right through the blossom end. Large beefsteak varieties are far more prone.
consequence: Ugly, entirely edible, and no threat to the plant. Cut the scar out and eat the rest.
look_alikes: Blossom end rot is a defined sunken patch on the bottom of an otherwise normal fruit; catfaced fruit is deformed all over.
monitoring: Nothing to do -- it is decided weeks before the fruit is visible.
prevention: Do not set transplants out into cold weather, which is the most common trigger. Avoid heavy nitrogen at flowering. Choose smaller-fruited varieties where late frosts are common. Avoid herbicide drift, which also causes it.
organic_controls: None needed. Cut out the scar.
chemical_controls: None.
treatments: Plant out into warm weather and go easy on nitrogen at flowering; the fruit is edible -- cut the scar off.

name: Bolting
description: The plant switching from leaf to flower, triggered by day length, by heat, or by a cold check early in life. It is the plant doing exactly what it evolved to do, at the moment you least want it.
signs: A central stem shooting up fast, leaves becoming small, narrow and bitter, and then flower buds. In coriander it happens in a fortnight in hot weather.
consequence: The crop is over. Leaves turn bitter and tough within days and do not come back.
look_alikes: Nothing -- it is unmistakable once you know it. Aster yellows also distorts the top but yellows and twists rather than elongating cleanly.
monitoring: Watch for the centre of a lettuce or a spinach starting to rise. Harvest that day.
prevention: Sow at the right time for the crop -- most of these are spring and autumn crops and fail in midsummer whatever you do. Choose slow-bolt varieties, which for lettuce and coriander are genuinely different. Shade cloth in hot weather. Keep water even; drought stress brings it on. Do not check transplants with cold, which triggers bolting in brassicas and onions later.
organic_controls: Harvest immediately at the first sign. Let a coriander or a brassica bolt on purpose for the seed and for the beneficial insects that work the flowers -- that is one of the cheapest things a garden can do for its own aphid control.
chemical_controls: None.
beneficials: The flowers feed hoverflies, parasitic wasps and lacewings, which is a good reason to leave one bolted plant standing.
treatments: Right season, slow-bolt varieties, shade and even water; once it starts, pick it all today.

name: Poor pollination
description: Cucurbits carry separate male and female flowers and need an insect to move pollen between them; sweet corn is wind-pollinated and needs a block of plants rather than a row. Without enough pollen the fruit starts and then aborts.
signs: Small fruit that yellows at the blossom end, shrivels and drops when a few centimetres long. Misshapen, pinched cucumbers and melons. Corn ears with scattered bare patches where no kernel formed.
consequence: No crop from those flowers. Easily and often misdiagnosed as disease, and treated with sprays that make it worse by killing the pollinators.
look_alikes: Blossom end rot blackens the blossom end of a fruit that keeps growing. Pickleworm leaves frass. An aborting unpollinated fruit is clean, small and simply yellows.
monitoring: Watch the flowers in the morning: are there bees in them? The first male flowers on a squash appear a week or more before the first female, and a run of female flowers with no males open is a common and self-correcting cause.
prevention: Plant sweet corn in a block of at least four short rows, never a single long one. Plant flowers that bring pollinators to the garden. Do not spray insecticides on open flowers, morning or otherwise. Avoid excess nitrogen, which delays female flowers.
organic_controls: Hand-pollinate: pick a male flower, strip the petals, and brush the anther against the stigma of a female flower in the morning. It works reliably and takes seconds. Shake sweet corn tassels over the silks on a still morning.
chemical_controls: None, and any insecticide applied to open flowers actively causes this problem.
beneficials: Bees of every kind -- this is the entry where the pollinator warnings on every other entry pay off.
treatments: Hand-pollinate in the morning; plant corn in a block; keep sprays off open flowers and grow flowers for the bees.

name: Nutrient deficiency
description: Not one problem but several, and the value of naming it is that it is what most pest sprays are wasted on. Which leaves go yellow first is the diagnosis: a mobile nutrient is moved out of old leaves to feed new ones, an immobile one is not.
signs: Nitrogen: uniform pale yellowing of the OLDEST leaves first, whole plant pale and slow. Magnesium: yellowing between the veins of older leaves with the veins staying green. Iron: the same pattern but on the YOUNGEST leaves, and usually a pH problem rather than a shortage. Phosphorus: dull dark green with purple stems and undersides, and stunting, common in cold soil in spring.
consequence: Slow growth and a small crop. Rarely fatal, but months of a plant not doing what it should.
look_alikes: This is the one everything else is mistaken for. Spider mites stipple but have webbing; viruses mottle but distort the growing point; root problems wilt in the afternoon. Check the roots and the leaf undersides before feeding.
monitoring: Look at which leaves are affected before doing anything: oldest first means a mobile nutrient, youngest first means an immobile one or a pH problem. A soil test once every few years settles what guessing cannot.
prevention: A soil test, then compost and a balanced feed according to it. Get the pH into range -- most vegetables want 6.0 to 7.0, and outside that band nutrients that are present become unavailable, which is why iron chlorosis is usually a pH problem. Do not feed cold soil in spring and expect a response.
organic_controls: Compost, well-rotted manure and a balanced organic fertiliser. Foliar feeds give a quick short-lived response and are useful for diagnosis. Warmth solves most spring phosphorus symptoms without any input at all.
chemical_controls: Soluble fertilisers work quickly and are easy to overdo; excess nitrogen makes soft growth that aphids and diseases prefer. Follow a soil test rather than a habit.
treatments: Read which leaves are affected first; get a soil test and fix the pH; compost and a balanced feed -- not a spray.

name: Herbicide drift and contaminated compost
description: Growth-regulator herbicides drifting from a neighbouring lawn or field, or -- more insidiously -- surviving through hay, straw, manure and compost. Aminopyralid and clopyralid pass through an animal and through composting intact and can persist for years in a bed.
signs: Fern-like, cupped, twisted or strap-like new growth with parallel veins, on tomatoes, beans and potatoes first, which are the most sensitive. The plant is not spotted or mottled, just contorted. Everything in one part of the garden, or everything grown in one batch of compost.
consequence: Plants that never crop, and a bed that can stay affected for one to three years if the source was contaminated compost or manure. This is one of the most expensive mistakes available to a gardener.
look_alikes: Mosaic virus mottles as well as distorting, and moves plant by plant. Aster yellows yellows and produces green flowers. Herbicide damage affects everything in an area at once, in a direction, with no mottling.
monitoring: If several unrelated plants distort at the same time, look at the pattern on the ground -- a gradient from one edge is drift, a whole bed is the compost.
prevention: Test any bought compost, manure or straw before spreading it: sow beans or peas in a pot of it against a pot of known clean mix and compare after three weeks. Ask what the hay or pasture was sprayed with. Do not spray herbicide on a windy day, and never use a sprayer that has held a herbicide for anything else -- there is no way to clean it well enough.
organic_controls: For the contaminated bed: nothing quick. Keep it cropped with grasses and sweet corn, which tolerate these herbicides, keep it moist and biologically active, and wait. Do not spread the material any further.
chemical_controls: None. This IS the chemical.
treatments: Bean-pot test any bought compost or manure before spreading it; grow corn and grasses on an affected bed and wait it out.

name: Transplant shock
description: A plant moved from a sheltered tray to open ground loses more water through its leaves than damaged roots can replace, and is at the same time meeting full sun and wind for the first time. Both halves are avoidable.
signs: Wilting for several days after planting, leaf edges scorched or bleached white, growth stalled for a fortnight, sometimes leaf drop. Worst on a bright windy day.
consequence: A checked plant that yields later and less, and sometimes never really catches up. Cold-checked brassicas and onions go on to bolt.
look_alikes: Cutworms sever the stem. Damping off pinches the stem base. Root maggots kill the roots. Look at the stem and the roots before assuming shock.
monitoring: Watch new transplants morning and evening for the first week. Wilting at midday that recovers by evening is normal; wilting in the morning is not.
prevention: Harden off over seven to ten days -- Carl records the schedule and counts the days for exactly this reason. Plant in the evening or on a dull day, never at midday in the sun. Water in thoroughly at planting to settle the soil around the roots. Do not tear the root ball apart. Shade for the first two or three days. Do not plant a heat-loving crop into cold soil.
organic_controls: Shade cloth or an upturned pot for the first days. Water in well and then keep the soil evenly moist rather than flooding it. Pinch off any flowers on a checked transplant so it puts its energy into roots.
chemical_controls: Root stimulant products are mostly dilute fertiliser and do not fix a hardening failure.
treatments: Harden off properly, plant in the evening, water in, shade for a few days; pinch off early flowers.

name: Frost and freeze damage
description: Ice forming in plant tissue ruptures the cells. Tender crops are killed at the first touch of frost; hardy ones are unaffected and some are improved by it.
signs: Leaves water-soaked and limp, then blackened and papery within a day or two. Growing tips killed first. On fruit, sunken glassy patches. Damage is worst in low spots and in the open, and least under a tree or a wall.
consequence: Total loss of tender crops -- tomato, pepper, basil, squash, bean. Hardy crops such as kale, leek and parsnip are unharmed and taste better afterwards.
look_alikes: Herbicide drift and disease can also blacken growth, but frost affects everything tender in an area on one night and leaves the hardy plants beside them untouched.
monitoring: Carl carries the forecast on the menu and the frost reminder is one of the thirteen kinds; the average last and first frost dates for your county are on the Calendar. A clear, still, dry night after a cold day is the dangerous one.
prevention: Plant tender crops after the last frost date for your county and get them out before the first. Row cover or an old sheet over the crop on a forecast frost night, held off the leaves and reaching the ground so it traps soil heat -- plastic touching a leaf makes it worse. Water the soil in the afternoon before a frost, which holds heat. Avoid low-lying frost pockets for tender crops.
organic_controls: Cover, harvest, or accept it. Do not cut back frost-damaged perennials until spring, since the dead growth protects the crown.
chemical_controls: None.
treatments: Cover with fabric down to the ground on a forecast frost; water the soil beforehand; pick everything tender first.

name: Heat stress
description: Above about 35C most vegetables stop photosynthesising efficiently, close their pores to save water, and stop growing. What looks like a watering problem is often a temperature problem that no amount of water will fix.
signs: Wilting in the afternoon that recovers by evening even in moist soil. Leaves cupping or rolling upward to reduce the surface facing the sun. Flowers dropping. Lettuce turning bitter, tomatoes not setting.
consequence: A pause in growth and cropping through the worst weeks. Rarely fatal to an established plant, and it resumes when the weather breaks.
look_alikes: Wilting that does NOT recover overnight is a root problem or a wilt disease, not heat. Physiological leaf roll is smooth and green; virus leaf curl yellows and stunts.
monitoring: Carl records the temperatures and the ET0; a run of days above 35C explains most of what looks wrong in July.
prevention: 30 to 50 per cent shade cloth over the worst weeks, which is the single most effective intervention. Heavy mulch to keep soil temperature down. Deep, less frequent watering so roots go down. Heat-tolerant varieties for the crops that matter. Plan the calendar around the heat rather than fighting it.
organic_controls: Shade, mulch, deep watering and patience. Do not fertilise a heat-stressed plant, which asks it to grow when it cannot.
chemical_controls: Anti-transpirant sprays have limited and inconsistent effect. Shade cloth does more for less.
treatments: Shade cloth, deep mulch and deep watering; do not feed it; wait for the nights to cool.

name: Waterlogging and root rot
description: Roots need air. Soil that stays saturated has none, the roots suffocate and die, and the water moulds move into the dead tissue. It is easily mistaken for underwatering, and treated by watering more.
signs: Yellowing lower leaves and wilting in soil that is plainly wet. Soft brown mushy roots instead of firm white ones. A sour smell from the soil. Algae or moss on the surface, and fungus gnats in a container.
consequence: The plant dies, and the diagnosis is usually wrong until it is too late. This is the commonest way a container-grown vegetable is killed.
look_alikes: Drought wilts in dry soil; this wilts in wet soil, which is the whole distinction. Fusarium and Verticillium wilt stain the stem interior; waterlogging does not.
monitoring: Put a finger in the soil to the second knuckle before watering anything. That is the test, and it is better than any schedule.
prevention: Check the soil before watering rather than watering on a timetable. Drainage holes in every container, and never a saucer left standing full. Raised beds or ridges on heavy clay. Add organic matter, which improves drainage in clay and retention in sand. Water deeply and less often.
organic_controls: Stop watering and let the soil dry. Improve drainage. Repot a container plant into fresh mix, trimming off the rotted roots. Carl records the watering and the rainfall -- read them together before deciding a plant is thirsty.
chemical_controls: Fungicidal drenches for root rot do not fix drainage, and drainage is the problem.
treatments: Feel the soil before watering; fix the drainage; let it dry out; trim rotted roots and repot a container.

name: Tipburn
description: The same calcium-transport failure as blossom end rot, in a leaf instead of a fruit. Fast growth in warm weather outruns the plant ability to move calcium to the leaf margins, which are the last place it reaches.
signs: Brown, dry, scorched margins on the youngest inner leaves of a lettuce or a cabbage head -- inner, which is what distinguishes it. Bacterial rots move into the dead tissue afterwards.
consequence: The head is unusable if the damage is inside it. Mostly a warm-weather and fast-growth problem.
look_alikes: Salt or fertiliser burn scorches the OLDEST outer leaves. Tipburn is on the youngest inner ones.
monitoring: Cut a sample head in warm weather rather than waiting for harvest, since the damage is inside.
prevention: Even watering; the swings are what cause it. Avoid heavy nitrogen, which forces the growth that outruns the calcium. Choose tipburn-tolerant varieties. Grow the crop in its proper season and harvest before a heat wave. Shade cloth in warm weather.
organic_controls: Even watering, moderate feeding, right season, prompt harvest.
chemical_controls: Calcium sprays are usually ineffective for the same reason as with blossom end rot: the calcium does not reach the tissue that needs it. Even water does more.
treatments: Even watering, moderate nitrogen, tolerant varieties, harvest before the heat.

name: Deer
description: The largest thing that eats a garden, and the one where every half-measure fails. A deer will clear a bed of beans, lettuce and young fruit trees in a night and come back the next.
signs: Plants browsed off at 60 to 180 cm with a ragged, torn end -- deer have no upper front teeth and tear rather than cut. Cloven hoof prints. Piles of pellet droppings. Rubbed and stripped bark on young trees in autumn.
consequence: Whole crops removed overnight, repeatedly, and young trees killed by rubbing. Deer also learn a route and return to it.
look_alikes: Rabbits cut cleanly at a 45-degree angle and only below about 60 cm. A ragged tear above knee height is a deer.
monitoring: Look for the tear rather than the missing plant, and look at the height. Tracks in soft ground after rain tell you where they come in.
prevention: A fence is the only reliable answer. Two metres, or two shorter fences a metre apart, since deer jump high or wide but not both. Electric fencing baited with peanut butter works well for a garden. Everything else buys time.
organic_controls: Repellents based on putrescent egg solids or capsaicin work for a few weeks and must be rotated and reapplied after rain, because deer habituate to any one of them. Motion-activated sprinklers are genuinely effective on a small garden. Netting or cages over individual beds. A dog.
chemical_controls: Repellents only; there is no chemical control and none would be legal or appropriate.
treatments: Fence properly, or accept the loss. Rotate repellents and use motion sprinklers as a stopgap.

name: Rabbits
description: Rabbits eat seedlings, beans, lettuce, brassicas and peas, working from the edges of a bed, and gnaw bark from young trees in winter.
signs: Stems cut cleanly at a sharp 45-degree angle, as if with secateurs, below about 60 cm. Round pellet droppings. Bark gnawed off young trunks in a neat band at snow height.
consequence: Rows of seedlings removed and young trees girdled and killed. Damage is concentrated near cover -- brush piles, long grass, sheds.
look_alikes: Deer tear rather than cut and reach much higher. Voles gnaw bark at or below ground level with fine parallel tooth marks.
monitoring: Look at the cut angle and the height, which settles rabbit against deer immediately.
prevention: A metre of chicken wire with 25 mm mesh, buried or pinned 15 cm into the soil at the base and turned outward, is close to complete and permanent control. Hardware cloth cylinders around young tree trunks. Remove brush piles and cut long grass near the beds so there is no cover to run to.
organic_controls: Fencing is the answer and everything else is a delay. Repellents work briefly. Row cover protects seedlings through the vulnerable weeks.
chemical_controls: Repellents only.
beneficials: Hawks, owls, foxes and snakes -- all of which want the cover kept short too.
treatments: Chicken wire a metre high with the base turned out into the soil; wire cylinders on young trunks; remove the cover.

name: Voles
description: Small rodents that live in runways under mulch, long grass and snow, eating roots, tubers and bark. They are almost never seen, and the damage appears all at once when a plant is lifted or when the snow melts.
signs: Surface runways about 5 cm wide in grass and under mulch, with small round holes. Bark gnawed from trunks at ground level with fine irregular tooth marks running in all directions. Potatoes and root crops hollowed out. Whole plants that pull up with no roots.
consequence: Fruit trees girdled and killed over one winter, and root crops destroyed. The damage is often discovered months after it happened.
look_alikes: Mole tunnels are raised ridges and moles eat insects, not roots -- a mole in a garden is usually eating grubs. Rabbit bark damage is a clean band with larger tooth marks.
monitoring: Pull mulch back in a few places in late autumn and look for runways. Check the base of young trees when the snow goes.
prevention: Keep mulch pulled back 15 to 30 cm from the trunks of trees and shrubs, which is the single most effective measure. Mow and keep grass short around the garden. Hardware cloth cylinders around young trunks, pushed into the soil. Clear weedy cover in autumn before they move in.
organic_controls: Habitat: short grass, mulch off the trunks, no long weedy edges. Snap traps set in the runways under a cover work well in a garden. Encourage owls and hawks with a perch.
chemical_controls: Rodenticide baits are available and are hazardous to pets, children and predatory birds; habitat management and traps are the better answer in a garden.
beneficials: Owls, hawks, foxes, snakes, cats.
treatments: Mulch pulled back off trunks, short grass, wire cylinders on young trees; snap traps in the runways.

name: Squirrels and birds
description: Squirrels take one bite from a tomato and leave it, dig up transplants and strip sweet corn. Birds peck ripening fruit and pull up newly sown seed and seedlings.
signs: A single bite out of each ripening tomato, and the rest left on the ground. Corn husks pulled back and kernels eaten. Neat holes pecked in ripe fruit. Freshly sown rows dug or pulled up.
consequence: Ripe fruit lost one at a time, sowings pulled up, and the corn crop taken in the week it was ready. Maddening rather than fatal, and very hard to stop by half measures.
look_alikes: Rats also take fruit but usually at night and gnaw more thoroughly. Slug damage has slime.
monitoring: Watch what happens the week fruit starts colouring; that is when it starts.
prevention: Netting or a fruit cage is the only thing that reliably works. Bird netting over a strawberry bed, held clear of the fruit on hoops so nothing can reach through and nothing gets tangled in it. Paper bags or mesh sleeves over ripening corn ears. Row cover over newly sown rows until they are up. Pick at first blush and ripen indoors.
organic_controls: Netting, sleeves and early picking. A shallow water source elsewhere in a dry spell genuinely reduces fruit pecking, because much of it is thirst. Reflective tape and scarers work for about a week each and then stop.
chemical_controls: None appropriate. Repellents do not last on fruit you intend to eat.
beneficials: The same birds eat a great many caterpillars; the goal is to keep them off the fruit, not out of the garden.
treatments: Net properly and hold it clear of the fruit; sleeve the corn ears; pick at first blush; put out water in a dry spell.
